utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, while the witness is being brought in, I noted -- note that yesterday a motion was received to amend the Rule 65 ter submission of the second accused. You may not have had a chance to look at it yet, but it is a matter we could, I think, deal with orally without any great formality once you've had a chance to do that. So if you would perhaps let us know when you're in a position to clarify your own reaction, we would be able to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, I was aware we had it; we just haven't had a chance to look at it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will now continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. I think when we left off yesterday I asked you whether the autonomous province were federal units and you explained to me that they were not, but I had a question for you. In Yugoslavia in 1989 and 1990, the autonomous provinces did have representatives who were members of the collective Presidency, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, one each, the same as all the other republics that were federal units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to ask you about an exhibit that Mr. Zecevic showed you yesterday it was -- or I guess it was on Monday. It was Exhibit 1D370, and I'm sorry I don't recall what the tab number is. It's in the grey binder, I think it's in the grey binder, volume 1. I see it appears to be tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 8, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it is the Law on Amendments of Certain Laws And Regulations dated the 8th of March, 1993. And as I understand your testimony, Professor, this was an example of some 25 laws that were being changed to harmonize the laws with the changes brought about as a result of the new Constitution in the Republic of Serbia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you look at article number 2 to that law. I think Article 2 deals with the law regarding the -- I don't have the term of art in front of me, but it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, if we can go to Article 2 in e-court, I think it's the next page of this document. I see Article 2 in the Serbian version, but the English I think we have to go back one page. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Article 2 is the Law on Termination of the Activity of the Assembly of the autonomous -- or the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo. And that law was going to cease to be valid once an Assembly was constituted. Professor, was a -- was an Assembly in Kosovo ever reconstituted after 1989?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an Assembly in 1989; it ceased to operate in 1990, following the unilateral enactments by the Albanians who were in the Assembly. I'm talking about enactment on putting Kosovo and Metohija on an equal footing with all the other federal units, whereby they wished to become a federal unit themselves. The Constitutional Court declared this to be unconstitutional, and that's why it lost all validity. And that is why the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia adopted this Law on the Termination of the Activity of the Assembly of the SAP of Kosovo and the Executive Committee of the SAP of Kosovo. From that moment on, the Kosovo and Metohija Assembly was not reconstituted for the simple reason that the Albanians boycotted the elections. They refused to take part in the elections to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which elections were those? Were there some elections actually scheduled to reconstitute an Assembly in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was regulated in the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution dated 1990. I mean, how autonomy was to be transformed to a 1990 constitution regime. There was to be a statutory ruling, I think this is paragraph 13 of the Law on Implementation of the 1990 constitution, or rather, the constitutional law on the implementation of the 1990 constitution, my apologies. However, this decision was never adopted. And that is why no elections were ever held again in Kosovo and Metohija. The Albanians boycotted the elections, and they were after all the majority population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after 1990 with the change in the constitution, Kosovo no longer had a constitution of its own, nor a Constitutional Court, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Under the 1990 constitution, Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija, neither of these autonomous provinces had any executive anymore, and by that very fact, this means they had no Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm unclear about your last answer, Professor. You said that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that under the 1990 constitution the autonomous provinces -- rather, neither of the autonomous provinces, Vojvodina nor Kosovo and Metohija no longer had any constitutional powers, no powers to adopt their own constitutions. They still had the power to adopt a statute as the supreme legal act. By this very fact, the need ceased for the Constitutional Court to exist because the Constitutional Court defended the laws and regulations of the autonomous provinces. But since the autonomous provinces had no executive or legislative power anymore, there was no need for either of them to actually have a Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It wasn't on that matter, it was on the matter of the elections. You said there was to be a statutory ruling, and you thought it was paragraph 13 of the Law on Implementation of the 1990 constitution, but this was never adopted. Now, that would have been the responsibility of the Serb Assembly, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, if you look at Article 2, which is the one that we have before us, the Law on Termination, certain laws, Article 2, paragraph 2, reads: "The Assembly of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija shall be constituted after the conduct of a direct and secret ballot in accordance with the provisions of the constitution and a provisional statutory decision issued by the National Assembly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do I take it from that that the National Assembly failed to ever issue a provisional statutory decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The National Assembly never adopted that provisional statutory decision for the simple reason that parallel authorities, parallel bodies of government, parallel institutions generally speaking were soon created in Kosovo and Metohija since the Albanians now refused to recognise the Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, were you ever asked by anyone to prepare a draft statute for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a draft statute was prepared. If you remember the delegation of the Republic of Serbia that we spoke about yesterday, starting on the 12th of March, 1998, the delegation travelled to Pristina with this draft and with a draft law on local self-government. However - and we did say a thing or two about that yesterday - the representatives of the majority Albanian parties failed to show up; they never responded to those invitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that draft then was first prepared in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Draft was first prepared as early as 1990 and 1991. However, it was never used for the reasons that I have been enumerating. The Kosovar Albanians boycotted the work of the state institutions and they publicly stated that they did not recognise the institutions of the Serbian state as their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I guess I'm not clear on that, though. As I read Article 2 here, a provisional statutory decision was to be issued by the National Assembly. Couldn't the National Assembly have done that without any participation by the Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, in theory the National Assembly could have done that, but this would be no more than dead letters on a page. The National Assembly never did this in agreement with the Kosovar Albanians. However, they boycotted the entire effort, saying that they were not interested in this sort of autonomy, which in their eyes was less than a proper autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It was certainly less than what they had prior to 1990, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was less, although in comparative terms, if you look at Europe, this is actually far more. There is no autonomy in the world that enjoys executive powers, that enjoys its own legislation or independent judiciary. There is no autonomous province in the world without the consent of which you can change the constitution of a country, of a state. There is no such autonomy in the world. I don't think there will ever be. This was a form of constitutional excess in a manner of speaking that such autonomy was, in fact, founded in the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. There's a transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, I didn't hear you because the interpreter was still speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, I understand, Your Honours. There is a problem in 6, 23, without the consent of which you cannot change the constitution -- maybe I'm getting wrong now. There is no autonomous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm really sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me follow-up on that then to be sure I understand. Prior to 1990 was the consent of the autonomous provinces required in order to change the Constitution of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under the 1974 constitution. The consent was, in fact, granted to have amendments to the law by constitutional amendments, amendments to the 1989 Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. Both of the autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosmet, gave their consent for these amendments to be made, the amendments having previously been adopted by a prescribed majority in the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so I understand correctly then, prior to the new constitution in 1990, the autonomous provinces, Kosovo and Metohija and Vojvodina, in effect had a veto regarding changes in the constitution. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And under the new constitution, after 1990 Kosovo and Vojvodina only had the opportunity to express an opinion or complain about a change, but they could not exercise a veto over proposed changes to the Constitution of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think that's all the questions I had on that exhibit at this time. I want to move on to -- I think it was at page 1289 -- 12889 from Monday, and you were talking about Article 9, paragraph 2 of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, where you indicated that the president didn't have executive power, that he did not have or does not have operational powers of the executive power. Those powers are with the government. But what about during a declared irregular state, such as a state of war, doesn't the president have some operational executive powers then?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During a state of war or an imminent threat of war, as we have seen, the president receives a proposal from the government, that is if the People's Assembly is unable to meet. He then adopts decrees, the sort that are normally adopted by the People's Assembly. It is his responsibility once the state of war is declared over to adopt these -- to submit these decrees to the People's Assembly for ratification. This is envisaged in Article 83, item 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the state of war, he actually is acting in the place of the National Assembly in issuing decrees, passing laws, in effect, no?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with the cabinet, and the cabinet consolidates the actual documents, he is the provisional legislator for as long as hardship continues to prevail in the country. But neither he nor the government can actually decide on any of the issues normally pertinent to the People's Assembly. Once the situation in the country is normalised, back to normal, the People's Assembly must ratify all of their proposals and decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions about that. You explained to us yesterday how the government would -- would draft the proposed decrees and give them to the president. Could he decide that he did not want to sign off on one of those proposed decrees; and if so, was there any remedy for the government who had proposed it or is the president in that situation the final arbiter about whether a decree will be issued or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can all see, if we look at the text, the constitution provided for no situation like that. It does not provide for the eventuality of the president failing to actually sign a draft decree submitted by the cabinet. No eventuality is envisaged should the president fail to sign a draft decree submitted by the National Assembly, proposed by the National Assembly. The president is expected to do both, though, both to adopt a decree agreed by the cabinet and also to promulgate a law previously adopted by the People's Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand in the context of normal situation during peacetime, and as I read the constitution that if the National Assembly passes a law and presents it to the president, he really doesn't have any option other than to exercise his suspensive veto or else promulgate the law, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if he failed to do either one of those two things, wouldn't he be acting in violation of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But during a state of war when he, in effect, is replacing the National Assembly, and it seems to me -- it does not seem to me, I guess, as clear that he does not have the option to refuse to issue a decree proposed by the government. Because in effect isn't he the one-man legislature?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I can't agree. It is government that in actual fact takes over the competences of the People's Assembly. It is the government that formulates the norms, whereas the president of the republic in actual fact merely gives his consent by signing off certain documents and he declares drafts by the government to be decrees or defines them as decrees. In creative terms, it is the government that assumes the powers of the People's Assembly. It is not the president who formulates the norms. It is the government that does this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What I gathered from what you had said yesterday, the government proposed these regulations to the president, and I guess for me in English using that word "propose" is something in the nature of a suggestion to, in general, someone with higher authority or a different authority. And they have the discretion to accept my proposal or reject it. Isn't that the relation between the government and the president during a state of war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the constitution provided for no such situation explicitly. Given the absence of such a decree, we can only speculate as to what the president might or might not have done. There is no such norm provided by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the provision we're looking at I think is Article 83, 7, and the wording is clear: "At his own initiative or at the proposal of the government during a state of war or an imminent threat of war, he can adopt instruments relating to matters falling within the competence of the National Assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, and I read that to say that he can adopt. So he may have a proposal from the government which he chooses not to adopt. It does not say he shall adopt at the proposal of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that a correct reading, Professor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, just a clarification. The wording of the Article 83, 7, says "donosi" [Interpretation] Adopts enactments, [In English] Takes, adopts decisions, adopts acts, not "can" or "shall." Maybe the translators can explain this. The wording says, if it can be translated, please: [Interpretation] "During a state of war or an imminent threat of war, shall adopt enactments in relation to matters pertinent to the People's Assembly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My concern, Mr. Hannis, was not so much with that, and if I've introduced the word "can," then I apologise for that. But my concern was with the initial words of subparagraph 7: "At his own initiative ..." Which would suggest that he could act without the authority of the government. Is that an accurate interpretation in your opinion, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. But Mr. Hannis asked me about the provisions contained in the binder. All these provisions were adopted at the proposal of the government. Not a single one was adopted at the initiative of the president. As far as the wording of the constitution is concerned, you are entirely right. He can move of his own accord or following a proposal by the government. However, all of the 16 provisions that we are debating here, now that is something that I believe Mr. Hannis was asking me about and all of these were adopted at the proposal of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And as far as you know, were there any proposed decrees presented to Mr. Milutinovic that he did not issue during a state of war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such proposed decrees did not exist, there were no such proposed decrees. Whatever decrees the government presented were confirmed by Mr. Milutinovic with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit P1862, and that is tab number 14 in the grey binder. This is the Law on the Government of the Republic of Serbia, dated 21 January 1991. And in particular I want to look at Article 18.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab 14, I believe, of the grey binder.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Article 18 of that law, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The English translation I have reads that: "During a state of war or imminent threat of war, the government shall propose to the president of the republic that he adopt documents on issues falling under the jurisdiction of the National Assembly." Again, for me in English, "propose" has a connotation of "suggest." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "propose" means not "suggest" in the sense that they only give him an impetus and he will then draft the text; it's rather the government that draws up the text and proposes to him that he adopt the text drafted by the government as the final document. So it's not the government that moves the president to draft documents or enactments. It's rather the government that establishes the content of that proposal. So when the government establishes a proposal, he is not free to make changes in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, but I read nothing in that article nor in the constitution that would prohibit the president from declining to accept the proposal. There's no specific prohibition against him refusing it, is there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't, just as there isn't in relation to promulgating laws. It is expected that the president will adhere to the letter of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But what we have in this situation is an absence of letters in the constitution on this issue, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. This matter is not regulated in the constitution, and precisely because it is not, I believe that the president of the republic when the government makes a proposal is duty-bound to promulgate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What do you base that belief on? Where do you find that? Is that just your personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It follows from the interpretation of the constitution. It says here: "Shall enact" not "may enact," so it's imperative, "shall enact." And secondly, the situation you are mentioning is not envisaged in the constitution at all. Had the constitution wanted the kind of situation you describe, it would have been stated in the constitution that the president of the republic may refuse to adopt a decree proposed by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it says "shall enact" and it shall enact those on his own initiative and those proposed by the government. What if something proposed by the government is 180 degrees opposite of a decree that the president wants to issue on his own initiative, then in the end isn't he the one who's the final arbiter?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president, as we said, according to the conception of the constitution, does not have executive power. According to Article 9, paragraph 3 of the constitution, it's the government that has executive powers. The president of the republic is not hierarchically superior to the government. The government issues decrees. Decrees are acts of the government. They fall within the competence of the government, and just as laws are promulgated by the president of the republic, so decrees which are, in fact, laws because they fall within the competence of the National Assembly, are adopted by the president of the republic. In the case of laws, he only promulgates, but because of the wartime conditions when it comes to decrees he adopts. Otherwise, if it -- if things were different, we would have a violation of the principle of division of power, which is explicitly stated in the constitution, the principle of the division of power -- excuse me. Sorry. Let me find it. It is expressly formulated in Article 9, which says that constitutional and legislative power belongs to the National Assembly, executive power belongs to the government, judiciary power belongs to the courts, protection of constitutionality and legality in compliance with the constitution belongs to the Constitutional Court, whereas the Republic of Serbia is represented and its unity expressed by the president of the republic. In my view, refusal to adopt a decree proposed to him by the government would constitute a violation of the principle of the division of power. It's quite another matter when he on his own initiative as expressly authorised by the constitution in Article 83, paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as a practical matter, Professor, how do you envision that would work then if the president took the view that you have stated, that if it's proposed by the government he really has to follow through on it and issue that proposed decree during a state of war, but he doesn't like it. So on Tuesday he issues the government decree, but on Wednesday he issues one directly contrary to it on his own initiative. What happens then? Because he wouldn't be acting in violation of the constitution. He issued the government decree that had been proposed to him, and under the constitution he is authorised to issue decrees on his own initiative which he does on Wednesday, which in essence nullifies the previous decree proposed by the government on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all possible in theory. That's just theoretical. Life is something else. A state of war or a state of an imminent threat of war is an exceptional situation in the life of any state, and under such conditions all the state organs aim -- aspire to the same goal. They are not mutually antagonistic. They are all coordinated. It's hard to imagine in a state of war for the government to go one way and the president another. There is a state of general mobilisation. All the forces, all the resources within the country aspire to the same goal, the goal of defending the country. So that, yes, in theory what you say is possible, but that's just theoretical. It's impossible to imagine such a situation in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Professor. Sometimes real life is different than what is possible when just looking at the paper. I want to ask you about Article 83, number 2 of the president's powers under the Constitution of Serbia, and this has to do, I believe, with his powers to appoint members to the Constitutional Court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did I understand your testimony correctly on Monday when you said in carrying out those duties or powers, the president has to reach an accord with the cabinet basically ahead of time on who those candidates are that he will then propose to the Assembly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm not sure whether you asked me whether he can appoint or nominate, propose, in other words, judges of the Constitutional Court. I don't see the transcript very well. If you ask me whether he can propose, you are right, yes; if you ask me whether he can appoint, the answer is no, he cannot appoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He can only propose, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he can only propose candidates for the presiding judge and the judges of the Constitutional Court. But he can nominate only, or rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He cannot nominate just those judges he likes, he feels would be good judges of the Constitutional Court, but those who get a majority in the Assembly. And in order to make sure of that, he has to consult at least the prime minister because it's the cabinet that controls the parliamentary majority. So he has to find out whether the persons he has in mind can gain the support of the majority in the National Assembly. Otherwise, he's being reckless if he doesn't ask the prime minister about that, he risks compromising both himself and the candidate he is nominating to the National Assembly. His proposal will not be passed. As I said, such a situation did occur when under this constitution President Boris Tadic made a proposal to the National Assembly, and one of the candidates he nominated was not passed by the Assembly and did not get the required majority to become a judge of the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if I understand correctly, that's a matter of practicality. Is the president required to only propose those that he knows in advance will be approved by a majority? He could nominate others, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. He can nominate whoever he likes, those he feels deserve to be nominated. But I told you what risk he would be taking. Theoretically, yes, he has absolute freedom to nominate whoever he likes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But it's not much of a power, is it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I have been trying to say. It's not much of a power available to the president of the republic, and even that he cannot do on his own, independently. It's only in theory that he's free to nominate whoever he likes. In practical terms, he's bound by the position of the majority in the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt here, please forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Learned Professor, I just wanted to ask a question for finding a fact. Now, besides the constitution in many countries, there are instruments like the rules of business with which the relationship between the various organs are regulated. And actually these rules of business derive their power from the constitution itself because they are enacted under the constitution. Because -- did you have any such rules of business, because then that would clarify the position what the president could do and what he could not do. Would you be kind enough in informing us about it. I'm grateful for this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand your question. While this constitution was in force, we had the Law on the Election of the President of the Republic. We had a Law on the Constitutional Court, a Law on Proceedings before the Constitutional Court and the legal force of its decisions. We had a Law on the Government, a Law on the State Administration, a Law on Courts. So all these institutions established by the constitution were regulated by laws. There was constitutional legislation to implement the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And because of these laws, obviously there was no room left for any confusion like a clash of two decrees about which our learned friend from the Prosecution spoke of. Because I think such laws or any rule of business would determine what the president would do and what he would not do in exercise of his powers; and once that is prescribed, there cannot be a clash.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The law only regulated the issue of the election of the president of the republic, because in the constitution that is not provided for in every detail. The constitution of 1990 says in Article 87, paragraph 7, that's the last paragraph, that the manner of election and revocation of the president of the republic shall be provided for by law. And as we saw yesterday, and Mr. Hannis also asked me about that, the powers of the president of the republic cannot be provided for by a law. They are only provided for by the constitution. So only what the constitution says can be regulated by legislation, can actually be regulated by legislation. So the powers of the president, the Assembly, the government, and the Constitutional Court cannot be regulated by laws. And there are articles to support everything I've just said now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. With regard to the specific hypothetical situation I had asked you about during wartime and a disagreement between the government and the president about what law they wanted to have issued, were there any specific provisions -- you've already said in the constitution there wasn't anything to address that possibility. Were there any specific rules of procedure or laws that dealt with that kind of possibility?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about the state of war. I think you told us previously how that can come about and who can declare a state of war. Who decides when a state of war is ended?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the Federal Assembly that decides when a state of war has ended, according to the constitution then in force. That's the constitution of 1992. Of course, if the National Assembly cannot be convened, it's the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The cabinet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you see that in Article 78, the constitution of 1992, paragraph 3. "The Assembly shall decide on war and peace, declare a state of war, an imminent threat of war, and an state of emergency." And Article 99, paragraph 10, says: "When the Federal Assembly is unable to convene, after hearing the opinion of the president of the republic and the president of the council of the Federal Assembly, the state of war or imminent threat of war" and so on, this is done by the federal cabinet. So once again, it's always the Assembly, and if the Federal Assembly is unable to meet, then it's the federal cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What's the role of the president of the republic in connection with ending a state of war, is he only to consult or advise the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the president of the Republic of Serbia, the president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the Federal Republic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The constitution does not give him any powers here except that he is consulted. In Article 96, which lists the powers of the president of the republic, he is not given any such power.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there any provision in the law for what happens if during a state of war the cabinet is not able to meet, the government's not able to meet, because I think you told us that was a body for some -- for example, in Serbia that was a body of some 30 people. How big a body was the cabinet of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the cabinet numbered fewer people by far. I think it was smaller by half or more than half. There were about ten ministers, presidents and deputy presidents. So the cabinet of the Federation was much smaller in numbers of members than the cabinet of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was no provision in the law that you're aware of to deal with the situation where the federal cabinet might not be able to convene because of the state of war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would have had to be mentioned in the constitution, because this is a constitutional issue that cannot be regulated by a law, and as we see there is no such provision in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. We were talking about the situation -- on Monday you were talking about the situation when once the National Assembly was able to meet again during a state of war or after the state of war ended, that the president was duty-bound to present to them those enactments that he had issued during the state of war for them to confirm, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does the National Assembly have the discretion to decline, to confirm all or some of those decrees, if they disagreed with any of them for some reason?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did have this discretion because this matter falls within its competence. All these decrees were enacted in so-called legislative matters, matters falling within the competence of the National Assembly. And the act of the National Assembly we had before us here in this file shows what the fate was of all the 16 decrees adopted by the president and what the National Assembly decided in relation to each of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If, hypothetically speaking, the National Assembly decided not to confirm one or more of the decrees that had been issued during the state of war, what would be the consequences of that? First of all, any consequences to the president as a result of the Assembly declining to confirm the decrees he issued?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first question would be the responsibility of the cabinet. The cabinet had consolidated all of those proposals, the responsibility of the cabinet before the Assembly. I think the delegates could then move to have a vote of confidence for the government. But if they believe the president to have violated the constitution by adopting a decree like that, a one-third minority of the delegates had the right to start an investigation in the Assembly to look into this matter, whether, in fact, the president had violated the constitution or not. This is a political issue. This is not a legal matter. This is something for the delegates to decide. It is for them to judge whether the government made a political mistake or perhaps the president of the republic. And then in the case of the government or the cabinet, they can have a vote of confidence or no confidence if it was the president who was found to be in the violation of the constitution, it's up to the Assembly to judge the matter. Should the Assembly find that the president violated the constitution, then there is a referendum and the people of Serbia, the voters, can have a vote in order to recall the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what would be the fact regarding any decrees that had been issued by the president during the state of war, which the National Assembly later declined to confirm, what would be the practical fact of what had been done in connection with those decisions? I take you back to our discussion about General Lukic's promotion and the subsequent finding by the Constitutional Court that that law under which the promotion was given was an unconstitutional extension of the president's powers.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm under the impression that I explained the decision of the Constitutional Court. This is only for future use from the moment the decision is published, from that moment on. That's how it works. As for the National Assembly, the National Assembly can, for example, conclude that a decree adopted during the state of war is no longer in force once the state of war is declared over. If they believe the decree to have been unconstitutional or illegal, they can move the Constitutional Court to establish the legality or constitutionality of such a decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now I want to move back to the constitution once more and Article 135. We've talked about the provisions that were in the constitution regarding armed forces of Serbia and matters relating to dealing with foreign affairs and what you've termed, I think, reserve competences that were put in in anticipation of a possible constitutional vacuum occurring in light of the -- what seemed to be possible secession of some of the republics from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time. And you've agreed with us that that was an unusual provision for a constitution. And at the time the commission wrote that constitution and put in that provision, you - and I mean you all in the commission - you knew that was in violation of the federal constitution and you say so in the article, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you certainly intended for that to be the case. Wasn't that rather unconstitutional of you, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is unconstitutional from the point of view of the federal constitution. But if you go back to Roman law it says, "divisa inter arma silent leges" [sic]. As a time of danger of war, the laws are silent. That's what it means. This was a factual political situation, and what Serbia was supposed to do was to prepare itself in terms of norms, the constitution, and laws for a situation where Yugoslavia as a federation was simply no longer around. In 1990, September in 1990, Serbia adopted its constitution. In 1989, Slovenia adopted amendments to its own laws to amend federal laws and the federal constitution. The situation became highly irregular. There was a lot of disruption. The hierarchy, the implicit hierarchy between the various laws was no longer complied with. Croatia started the same process by adopting its own constitution the same year as Serbia. You are entirely right, I must say. That is what the situation is in the eyes of a lawyer, but the facts of life dictated a different course at the time, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. But if Yugoslavia actually did dissolve and Serbia became independent, at that time it would and could have all these powers, all these reserve competencies, and more if it wanted, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could in terms of its laws, in terms of its constitution. Serbia would be prepared to meet the situation head on. That was one of the reasons the constitution was adopted. That was one of the reasons the provisions were phrased the way they were, especially Article 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So I guess my question is: If Serbia would be able to, in the event of the actual dissolution of the republic, Serbia would be able to have its own constitution with all these competencies, why was it necessary to put it in the constitution in 1990? Because it was clearly unconstitutional in the sense that it was contrary to the federal constitution. Why was it decided to do it that way?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reasons are the same as before. I believe I've explained the reasons already. The reason is to defend Serbia from a possible secession and the future events bore this out. There were republics that wanted to break away from the Yugoslav Federation. In this case, Serbia would have been left without a constitution regulating some vital issues. Who is in charge of the country's defence? Who is in charge of the country's foreign affairs? There would have been a whole number of different areas not regulated by the constitution. This was all a job for the Federation or had been up to that point. And now Serbia had this new constitution regulating these issues for the eventuality that the Federation should one day cease to exist. And indeed in 1992, four of the six original federal units left the Federation and became independent states. The remaining two re-organised themselves as a dual Federation, a two-member Federation. And the rest was what Article 135 said it should be. It was to be expected that Serbia would then bring its constitution in harmony with the 1992 constitution of the Federation. However, Article 135 dictated that the shelf-life in a manner of speaking of the 1990 constitution be extended. It was still in force in 2003 when the constitutional charter was adopted and continued to apply until as late as 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How -- how do you think the authorities in Serbia would have reacted if in 1989, Kosovo or Vojvodina had changed their constitutions to have a provision analogous to this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither were subjects of the Federation. Article 2 of the 1974 constitution lists six federal units, not including Kosovo or Vojvodina. Kosovo and Vojvodina were parts of the Republic of Serbia; therefore, they could not secede from the Federation. They could only have tried to secede from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you have to be patient with me, Professor, because I'm an outsider and a layman about much of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you pursuing this? Because that didn't answer the question you put.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not, Your Honour. If you have a question you want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question, Professor, wasn't about the relationship between Kosovo or Vojvodina and the Federation; it was about the relationship between Kosovo and Vojvodina with Serbia. So if a similar provision relating to the powers of a republic rather than a federation had been included in the Constitution of Kosovo, if they decided to amend their constitution, how would the Republic of Serbia have reacted was the question. Can you address that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Constitutional Court of Serbia would have ruled this to be unconstitutional, since it would not have been consistent with the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, under which the Republic of Serbia should have within its composition two autonomous provinces. The Federation never ruled the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia to be unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: During the period from 1989 until 1999, was there a Constitutional Court in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was one in 1989. It was organised in compliance with the 1974 constitution. As of 1990, it was organised along the lines of the 1990 constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it was properly constituted and in working order between 1990 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was. It was throughout, with the exception of the year of 2000. No new members were appointed to the Constitutional Court, and for a brief period, just over a year, the previous judges had retired so the Constitutional Court did not have a sufficient number of members to proceed with its normal activities and that was in 2000. The situation went on for about one year and four or five months; I'm not entirely certain about the exact duration. For example, as we speak, the Constitutional Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That answers the question. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So Article 135 in the insertion of these reserve competences, to me as an outsider it seems that given the circumstances at the time, in some ways this provision could be seen by the Federal Republic or some of the other member republics as, in some way, a threat on the part of Serbia. In essence they're saying, Look, we can have our own army and we're ready to go if this Federation isn't going to hold together. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia did not have an army; there was only a JNA. The JNA was the Army of the Federation, it was in the federal constitution. This was something provided for by the federal constitution, the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. Professor, are you aware in 1989 and 1990, what was the ethnic make-up of the JNA? What percentage of the professional members of the JNA were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, I'm unable to answer that question. I'm no expert in military matters; I've never claimed to be one. I've never studied these matters. I simply don't know. I think you should look elsewhere to find someone who might be well-placed to answer these questions. I can only speculate, but that is meaningless to the work of this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I won't ask you to speculate. We will have other witnesses who can probably better answer that. Would you agree that it was a majority, that Serbs constituted a majority of the professional officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would have to object at this time. This -- I don't see how it is relevant and how this come out of the direct examination of the Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't need to come out of the direct examination. It's plainly relevant to the question of how prepared Serbia might have been to trigger these unconstitutional provisions in view of the dissolution of the Federation. And whether more than 50 per cent of the army were Serbs might have been a matter of common knowledge, it's a movement away from the original question. And if the witness feels that he cannot answer because it's not a matter of common knowledge, then he'll tell us. Please deal with the question, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that I'm unable to answer the question. I'm a scientist, a scholar. I base my views on facts, on specific information. I'm simply unable to answer this question. I never dealt in any military matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Who was the president of the Republic of Serbia in 1990 when the constitution was being amended?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia had no president in 1990; it had a Presidency. This was a collective body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there a president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mr. Slobodan Milosevic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when you testified in this case -- or in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic about some of these matters?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that -- I'm going to take you, Professor, specifically to the 20th of January, 2005, you were being asked some questions about [sic] Mr. Nice concerning Article 135 of the constitution, and particularly those reserve competencies including foreign relations and the president commanding the armed forces of Serbia. And Mr. Nice at page 35476 asked you this, and I quote: "You've told us on more than one occasion that you were merely a technician doing your drafting. So will you tell us, please, who instructed you to make provision for Serbia to have under the command of the president armed forces? Who instructed you to make that extraordinary provision?" That's at lines 6 through 10. There was some discussion, there was an intervention by Mr. Milosevic, and eventually, Mr. Nice asked again if he could have an answer. Judge Robinson then at page 35477 said to you, Professor: "Who gave you your drafting instructions, that's the question?" And, sir, your answer was: "I've understood it and the answer is just one word: Nobody." Do you recall being asked that question and giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I explained yesterday how the constitutional committee worked as a collective body, not just me as the person who drafted the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and I understand that. But I think we agree that this Article 135 is new and unusual, something that it seems would have stood out in your mind at the time. Do you recall now who first proposed including those provisions and what turned out to be Article 135?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember - and this was, after all, 17 years ago - this proposal for perfectly understandable reasons, facts of life, economic matters, was put forward by the then-president of the federal Executive Council, Mr. Stanko Radmilovic, but that's based on my recollection. I must underline that. He provided a very compelling explanation. You see, paragraph 2 talks about compensation. This was, above all, motivated by economic factors, economic development. You see what it says: "Should the equal rights enjoyed by the Republic of Serbia be jeopardized in any way or its interests and if no compensation is offered in return and this compensation is a category from the federal constitution, the republican bodies adopt certain enactments in order to protect their own republics." This is a defensive measure, you might say, this provision. Should there be any discrimination, should there be any sort of disintegration within the Federation itself, then these provisions adopted by the Republic of Serbia would take effect, but not before such time. The Republic of Serbia is entitled to adopt enactments in order to protect its interests should this mechanism of solidarity cease to function in terms of compensation. I believe I quoted the article from the 1974 constitution which defined the institute of compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a couple questions following on that answer. Tell us, Mr. Stanko Radmilovic, you say he was the then-president of the Federal Executive Council, is that for the Federal Republic --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the republican Executive Council. Did I say "federal"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It came out in the transcript that way. So the Republic of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The republican Executive Council, the Republic of Serbia. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to the provision about compensation, I can understand how he might have been one to bring that up, but are you saying he's the one who suggested including the provision about the president and commanding the armed forces of Serbia or having a provision for dealing with foreign affairs?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. That wasn't the sort of situation that he bore in mind. All he was talking about was the economy, and then when the committee met, it became clear how this situation was to be regulated in a complex way. Mr. Radmilovic talked about the economy, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you say when the committee came together, it became clear, are you talking about the coordinating committee, the smaller body?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, it was the coordinating committee that worded most of the provisions. At the plenary of the constitutional committee, amendments were made to the provisions by the verification committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that smaller committee, how did it become clear that you should have this unconstitutional article and include reserve competencies for having armed force and body to deal with foreign affairs? How did that become clear, who raised it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was clear at the time that not only Serbia's economy would be affected, but its defence as well and its foreign affairs. All these were matters not regulated by the then-constitution of Serbia. These were all federal matters. The position taken was that these matters should be resolved as well. For example, the Assembly decides on war and peace. This is not just about the president. This is also about the Assembly, it's about the cabinet. If you remember, a while ago we read out the article saying that the National Assembly shall decide on war and peace. How can the National Assembly decide on war and peace when the federal constitution says explicitly that these are matters for the Federal Assembly, the federal parliament, not the National Assembly. Therefore, this is not just about the institution of the president of the republic. This is about all of the state organs. These reserve competencies attached to each and every one of those, but it was in the interest of the Republic of Serbia, should there be cases of discrimination against it within the Federation or should the Federation start to fall apart or cease to exist altogether. The same conclusion would have been reached by any constitutional committee facing a country in that sort of plight, which was the plight of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time. Moves had been made for a secession by the other republics in adopting their new constitutions, and this was much before Serbia started doing anything about it, before the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia was ever adopted. It was not a secessionist constitution, quite the contrary in fact. It declares loyalty to the Federation and it talks about matters that are for the federal constitution to regulate. Should the interests of Serbia be jeopardized with no compensation offered in return, then republican organs would adopt enactments in order to protect the Republic of Serbia, any enactments that might prove necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, in that long answer I'm still not clear about if you can help us about who raised the issue of including a president having armed forces of Serbia to command in that new constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's been asked and answered. He stated the general's name for who proposed the amendments. I don't know why we're spending so much time going through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who was that, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The republican secretariat for constitutional issues, Mr. -- I think it was Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Radmilovic, I think, and he was said to be concerned only about the economy. So the question is perfectly legitimate and I repel that objection. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Professor, do you recall who raised that issue?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In connection with the powers of the state organs, not just the president of the Republic, let me repeat, because he is not the only one with such powers, it is also the National Assembly and the cabinet who had such powers. There was no author here. If you mean that this was Slobodan Milosevic, no, he did not interfere in the work of the constitutional commission. The constitutional commission had experts for constitutional matters, and every expert on constitutional matters would have ordered things in this way had his country been in the same situation as the Republic of Serbia was at the time. If he had any professional conscience and any degree of patriotism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That still doesn't answer the question. Are you not willing to answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, I certainly am willing to answer it. But it was not an individual, sir, it was a group, a collective. All of us dealing in these matters made this decision. The verification commission and the constitutional commission had more than ten members, so this was not done by an individual. There were several of us who drafted, formulated, reviewed, went to the commission, the members of the constitutional commission made their own proposals. I cannot answer if I'm expected to say this was done by an individual and his name is so-and-so because that was not the situation, there was no such individual in existence. There were several of us. I partly participated in formulating this, but there was more than one person doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of another similar constitution where this sort of defensive measure, as you call it, has been introduced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, with reference to the constitutions of the Federation, the federal states, I do not know any federal constitution with such provisions. And as I said, this provision is highly unusual for the constitution of a federal unit, but it expresses an irregular situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Professor, I guess that's why I'm persisting in this area. You indicate this was highly unusual for a constitution and it was an unusual situation and circumstance that you found yourself in at the time. But that's why it seems to me that this would be something more clear in your memory about how this developed because, sir, you were a professor of constitutional law and have been for many years. And it seems to me that in that field, this must have been some of the most exciting work and one of the most exciting times in your career, no, to actually be writing the new constitution and putting in a unique provision like this that was clearly unconstitutional but was created to try and deal with the peculiarities of the time and the circumstance. Professionally, that must have been extremely exciting for you, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professionally, yes, it was an exciting time, as you say. But in human terms it was quite understandable, or rather, it's quite understandable that the country should be defended, including being defended by constitutional means. In your country from 1861 to 1865, there was a civil war against secessionists. Here, instead of a civil war with weapons, we were waging war with constitutions, and I think we shed less blood than was shed between 1861 and 1865 in the USA. The situation was the same. You had a war between secessionists and those loyal to the federation, but the war was being waged by constitutional means, not by weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Don't misunderstand me, Professor, I mean no disrespect here. I think this was a very creative piece of drafting that you put in this constitution to deal with -- to try to deal with this situation, but it's for that very reason that I find it difficult to accept your answer that you really don't know who raised this up and this happened as a group. This is something that seems to me would have been very memorable for you. And in connection with that, I find it interesting that in your answer a little bit ago that you raised the issue about Mr. Milosevic and he didn't have anything to do with this. I had not asked you a question about that. I had not mentioned him, other than asking who was president of the Presidency at the time. It seems to me that that was a little bit of anticipatory defence on your behalf similar to the anticipatory defence of Article 135. Can you tell me now if you recall who raised the issue of including a provision about armed forces of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honours, this has been answered like third time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you were more concerned about the argumentative nature of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that also, Your Honour, but I'm paying attention to the fact that this would be really unacceptable at least for the third time. Your Honour has posed the question, Professor answered; now the question is posed once again. This is at least the third time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hear what you say, Mr. Zecevic, but it does seem an important question. Somebody must have said, Hey, we better deal with the army and position of the -- our foreign affairs. And all Mr. Hannis is trying to find out is who it was that initiated that discussion. Well, let's hear if there's any further recollection on the part of the Professor. Can you assist any further on this matter, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I owe you an explanation. I mentioned President Milosevic because you mentioned Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice wanted me to say that it was President Milosevic who issued the orders, and when you mentioned Mr. Nice that was why I mentioned President Milosevic. However, I assert with full responsibility that this was not done by an individual. It was the common opinion of all the experts working in the coordinating body. It's very hard for me to say with reference to any provision here the author of this provision is so-and-so. This is a collective piece of work. It was adopted by the National Assembly. Every deputy in the National Assembly was able to propose an amendment, a modification of this. Constitutions are drawn-up collectively. How do we know in your constitution who wrote each one of those seven articles, it was the participants of the Philadelphia Convention all those who were there, it was not any individual. Now you want me to tell you who the author is, well, the author is the collective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: My learned Professor, when you referred to the American constitution, we have the Federalist Papers which do indicate who wrote what because everybody's been scribbling and writing, and what were the objections made and who opposed and all that, and the difference between the Founding Fathers. Did you have such a notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we did not have such a document because we didn't have Hamilton, Madison and Jay. Had we had them, we would have written such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Did you write about those who differed like Hamilton, the dissenting notes, or was no record kept of such an important document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably, yes, probably the stenographic record would contain those. There is a stenographic record. As far as I can recall, it was kept in the case of the constitutional commission. I'm not sure whether in the case of the coordinating commission there were just notes taken or whether there were stenographic notes or records, but there are records I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But that record will be the trail to find out who said what and who proposed, and I think that is precisely what is being requested of your good self today. Can you recall of that? That's, I think, the point if there is a record, there's a trail. I'm grateful, learned Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Time for a break I think, Mr. Hannis. Professor we must, as usual, break at this time. Please go with the usher, and we'll see you again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, can you remind me where we find the list of members of the commission to amend -- to draft the constitution? Is there a document that sets out the list of members?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I don't believe we have presented it. But if Your Honours would want us, I can try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I just wanted to know the position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, I have a couple of questions before we resume the cross-examination. I think you gave us the membership of the commission dealing with the amendment -- dealing with the drafting of the constitution. Now, that was headed, was it, by the president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, that's right. As for the composition of the entire commission, it was published in this same Official Gazette, the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia, that is. So the list of the members of the constitutional commission was published; it was no secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, we didn't see that document in the course of your evidence, I think. That's -- I just want to be clear about that. We haven't seen the document here, and that may or may not matter. How many other members of the commission were politicians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, politicians, I think it was predominantly politicians. At the time when I became a member of the commission, I was engaged as a person who was from the profession. I was not in politics at all at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was a smaller group, remind me of the name of that group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That group was called the coordinating commission of the constitutional commission. The coordinating commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how many of the coordinating commission were politicians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the coordinating commission, except for the late Zoran Sokolovic and Slobodan Vucetic, I think there were no other politicians, actually. All the rest were professionals, people from the profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind us of their positions, Sokolovic and Vucetic, what positions did they hold then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sokolovic was at that time the president of the Assembly, and Mr. Vucetic was a member of the Presidency of the Republic -- yes, the Republic of Serbia or the Socialist Republic of Serbia -- the Socialist Republic of Serbia, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking these questions because to some it might seem that the decision to include these exceptional provisions in the constitution would have to be a political rather than a legal decision. Now, was it not a political decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I think that the entire constitution by its content is a political decision. First, certain political decisions are crystallised and then lawyers formulate them normatively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me put the question more specifically. Some might think that the idea of introducing these exceptional provisions if we confine our attention to them into the constitution, would have to be a political decision made in advance of the drafting rather than a spontaneous legal idea that might emerge in the course of the drafting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This decision, I'm quite sure of that, was not made side-stepping the constitutional commission and the coordinating commission of the constitutional commission. It was made there. Now, how was it made? During the course of working on the constitution, it became obvious that in real life such a situation may crop up, and now what would the response in the constitution be for that kind of a situation once it crops up? That is something that was seen spontaneously. It did not come from the outside, like the entire constitution. I told you. I just worked out the systematics of the constitution. I'm trying to say that I made the skeleton as to what the constitution is supposed to look like and what subjects it should include. As for the normative decisions, we all wrote them together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, let me follow-up on the questions from Judge Bonomy just for a moment. The coordinating commission, which was the smaller body, were all the members of the coordinating commission also named in the Official Gazette that named the entire constitutional commission?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire composition of the constitutional commission was certainly referred to in the Official Gazette. I'm sure of that. I saw that with my very own eyes, because as a member, of course, I got an excerpt from the Official Gazette. As for the coordinating commission, I'm not sure, but I am sure that in the stenographic notes from the sessions of the constitutional commission, I am sure that the coordinating commission's composition is written down there. Maybe it was also made public in the Official Gazette. I cannot claim the latter for sure, but the first, yes, because I saw it with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know where the stenographic notes of the constitutional commission would be today, in terms of being stored in an archive somewhere?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are certainly in the Assembly archives. That was not destroyed; that exists. As far as I know when on one occasion an excerpt from stenographic notes was requested, they were in some archives in Zeleznik, that is a neighbourhood on the periphery of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And the coordinating committee, I don't recall if you answered this already, who decided the membership of that and made the appointment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions were made by the constitutional commission, that is to say from its own ranks it created a very narrow team that would work on the constitution because the constitutional commission had tens of members, and it is difficult to expect a big team to work efficiently. Then it chose members of the verification commission -- I beg your pardon, the coordinating commission. And I repeat, it consisted of people who were professionally trained for that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Including a couple of politicians?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including, yes, a couple of them. But Slobodan Vucetic is a politician but is still professionally versed in these matters, very well-versed. Mr. Sokolovic did not have professional legal training, but he took -- he could take part in proposing solutions. He could not set the style because the man was not a lawyer, but even as far as politicians are concerned, they were not illiterate in such matters they were versed in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in connection with, I think, your last answer to Judge Bonomy's questions at the beginning of this session about whether this might have been a political decision made in advance regarding the insertion of these unusual provisions, Professor, you can't exclude the possibility that, although you claim this came up spontaneously in the coordinating commission, isn't it possible that one of the members of the coordinating commission may have introduced this in the discussions after having been asked to do so by someone outside the coordinating committee? You can't rule that out, can you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, at the time when this provision was being formulated, nobody attached this kind of importance to it. This provision became the centre of attention thanks to this court, to The Hague Tribunal. So the spotlights were cast by the Hague Tribunal on this particular provision. We had no idea that this provision had that kind of value, that it was one of capital importance in the constitution. We had focused on completely different issues, and that is how we spent most of our energy. Such importance is being attached to it here, but we who took part in writing the constitution simply did not attach this kind of importance to that provision. It was simply a response to a situation that existed in real life, not right from the point of view of norm, not right from the point of view of the nature of the Federation, but it was indispensable, it was inevitable. It was done by the other socialist republics, too, not all in all fairness but it started with the Republic of Slovenia. And quite simply, why would Serbia die in the beauty of the law or should the world go down the drain so that justice would prevail? Advantage was given to other values.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we were able to get the gazette list of the members of the entire constitutional commission, would you be able to identify from that list which of those members of the overall commission were also members of the coordinating commission?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I don't think I could get it quite right, but with the assistance of Mr. Slobodan Vucetic, I would certainly be able to establish who the members of the coordinating commission were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Actually, I remember some of the names, but I'm not sure that I will give you most of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
