utterances.text: Can you give me the ones that you remember now for sure?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that I remember that the secretary for legislation was there, Mr. Negovan Kljajic; then the -- I think he was then deputy secretary of the Assembly, Mr. Perisa Jovanovic; Mr. Vladan Kutlesic; and the three I mentioned, Mr. Zoran Sokolovic; Slobodan Vucetic; and I. There were certainly others, too, but I know the faces but I can't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that experience, Professor. The names you just gave us, Mr. Kljajic, Mr. Jovanovic, Mr. Kutlesic, by your description of a couple of them, it seems that they were politicians as well. I thought I understood from your earlier answer that there were only two politicians on the coordinating committee.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not politicians. Negovan Kljajic was a professional for legislation. He was in the republic secretariat for legislation. He was a civil servant, not a politician. Perisa Jovanovic, too, he also came from the Assembly administration. Also Mr. Kutlesic, he was in the secretariat for legislation, the federal secretariat, but they were civil servants, high-ranking civil servants, not politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for explaining that to me. Let me move on now to another topic. You mentioned on Monday at page 12938 that: "As a rule, the federal constitution takes precedence over the republican constitution." And I understand that as a general principle, but does that appear anywhere in the constitution or the laws of Yugoslavia or is that just a general legal principle?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is written down in the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in Article 115 in three paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Regarding Article 85 of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia from 1990, I think that's the provision that deals with the power of the president to request the government to state its position regarding certain issues within its own jurisdiction. Can you tell us how that works. Does the president have to make some sort of formal written request? Is that something he can just do orally? And tell us first how that works.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't really have to do with the constitution position. I don't know what word you used in English and I don't know what came through in the interpretation, but it really has to do with one's standpoint, one's position from that point of view, from his own field of work, from his own jurisdiction. The president of the republic asks the government to take views on matters from the purview of their own work, and they do that. Then this request is made in written form and a response is sent in writing as well. In the Law on the Government it is regulated in terms of time. A minimum deadline is given of 48 hours to the government for it to prepare that particular position. This position is prepared by the ministry concerned depending on the actual field of work from which the president requested the view of the government. This institute was used most often in the period of so-called cohabitation when the government majority came from one political party or one group of political parties and the president of the republic from a different political party, which was not within the parliamentary majority. This institute was used most of all by the current president, Mr. Boris Tadic. He most often asked the government to take views, to take a position, and in this way, he was trying to expedite government decisions. It was done -- I'm sorry, I misspoke. In this way, the public was informed that the president asked the government to take positions on currently topical issues from everyday life, say infectious diseases, droughts and so on and so forth. What does the government intend to do, what is the position of the government concerning such and such a matter. I don't remember that this article at the time when the president of the republic was from the same party and when this party has parliamentary majority as well, I don't remember whether this was used at that time, I don't know. But it seems to me that even if it was used, it must have been very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your testimony at page 12957, I understood you to say that this was something quite important for the president's work. Can you explain why you take that view, that this power was important?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was important for the president who has such limited powers according to Article 83 of the constitution that he is nevertheless in a position to communicate with the public. That when you look at the needs of the day, what the public is interested in, in this way he spurs the government to act. He is not only seeking information, mere information, although the whole thing is manifested as information. In this way, before the public he is bringing pressure to bear on the government, not sanctioned pressure, but anyway he is trying to get the government to act on burning issues. I cannot remember now exactly the issues that President Tadic asked the government to take a position on so that the government could defend themselves from such requests. This was more -- this was regulated in more detail in the new Law on the Government, which was adopted in 2005. However, since that's not the issue here, I really did not prepare for that. I did not bring that law along.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It seems to me in the context of the powers that the president is given under the constitution that this really is one of his best tools, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not agree with you and I'll tell you why. If he is not satisfied with the position taken by the government, the president of the republic, except for his personal dissatisfaction, does not have anything else at his disposal. He cannot ask the Assembly to recall the said minister or the prime minister. Quite simply, as I said, he can be dissatisfied with that. But he does not have any constitutional instruments available. He cannot censure the government or the minister concerned because of their positions. They have the freedom to take any position and the president of the republic can only get upset, nothing else. He doesn't have anything else in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. He cannot formally censure the government or demand that a minister be removed from his position, I understand constitutionally, he can't do that formally. He's a popularly elected president chosen by the people, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct. Well, the main value of that institution is precisely this high democratic legitimacy; that is to say, this symbolic meaning that is incorporated in this institution, not the strength of the powers that he has. The president of the republic is an authority by virtue of the fact that he has such great democratic legitimacy. He was elected by all the citizens. However, according to the constitution he is not a big power holder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in real life would you agree with me that a popular president mobilising the media and relying on his popularity that helped put him in office, on certain issues may be able to effectively bring out some changes in government policy simply by creating a fuss, asking the ministry to state their positions on certain difficult controversial matters, he may be able to actually effect some changes even though he doesn't have constitutional authority.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, you're quite right, but what is the underlying assumption? The underlying assumption is that he is the leader of a major political party. It is only a president who is the leader of a major political party, and if that party has a parliamentary majority at that or is the main factor in the governing coalition in the parliamentary majority, that is, and if the president in addition to that as a person has great charisma, well then that is possible. It is only then that it is possible. Otherwise, a president who is not the leader of a political party is handicapped. He doesn't have the same kind of political power that is extra-constitutional power at that. He doesn't have the same kind of power that the -- that a president who is the leader of a political party has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it in Serbia is there can be circumstances where in the course of its period in power a government becomes unpopular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are your answers not based on the assumption that the government is always popular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. A government can be highly unpopular, but it is certain of its existence for as long as it has a stable parliamentary majority. So it's a moral issue. A government, as long as it has a majority in the parliament, is in power. It will have to give an account of itself at the next elections and it can be sanctioned at the next elections when the opposition will win and take over. But it can operate even if it's highly unpopular, especially in our part of the world where people always criticise the government and think the government is always to blame for all misfortunes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, Professor, let me move on to Tuesday of this week, and early Tuesday we were talking about the oath that the president takes under the constitution. And I think you described it as a constitutional mechanism to implement the responsibility of the president to the citizens, is that correct, or were you referring to something else other than the oath?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my main point, my fundamental thesis which I've always held is that an oath is not a constitutional norm. This is also evident from the fact that it is placed in quotation marks. So this is a text that somebody else pronounces, not the constitution itself, that's one point. Another point is that an oath has a moral value. It has to do with credibility. Will the president of the republic be credible or not. The oath contains some values which are essential for any state, such as territorial integrity, sovereignty, of the state; protection of human and civil rights; defence of the constitution; maintaining peace, the welfare of citizens. But it's not the president of the republic who can in reality defend the sovereignty and territorial integrity of a country; this will be done by the armed forces. He is not the one who can protect human and civil rights. That's for the courts and the Constitutional Court to do. Also, the law will be defended by the courts and by the Constitutional Court. Welfare and prosperity will depend on the economy, also extra-economic activities. So if one looks at all the things that the president of the republic is taking an oath to protect, we can see that these are values in any state. But he cannot be held responsible for failure to achieve these values because he is not the one who can bring them about. He is only expressing his loyalty to those values, stating that he shares those values with most citizens. That was why I felt that the legal responsibility of the president of the republic cannot be based on failure to respect the oath. He can only have a moral and political responsibility based on failure to respect the oath. That's my position. I hope I've been successful in clarifying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me see. For example, what we were talking about earlier, the president's right to request the government to state its positions. In a situation where the popularly elected president is at odds with the government and perhaps an unpopular government over some particular issue, could the president sort of invoke his oath when making inquiries from the government and to the public say that, I am trying to uphold my constitutional oath to devote every effort to preserving the peace and the welfare of all citizens by asking the government to set forth its positions on, for example, the allegations of the international community about the VJ and the MUP using indiscriminate force in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how he can ask for that position from the government when command of the armed forces is not within the competence of the government. You see, he can ask for the position of the government only on those issues which fall within the competence of the government, as listed in Article 99. It is only --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take your point, Professor. What about --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Article 90, I mistook the article. Article 90, that's where the competencies of the government are enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take your point. If I were to modify my question and omit the VJ and only talk the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, what would your answer be?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president can ask the government to set out its standpoints, but let me repeat, he has no instruments at his disposal to make the government change its standpoints. All he can do, if it would affect public opinion, is to resign. That's all he can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How often can he request the government to state its positions? I mean, for example, the hypothetical I gave you, could he renew his request for the government's position on allegations about indiscriminate use of force or disproportionate use of force by the Ministry of Interior of Serbia against Kosovo Albanian civilians every time that there was a new report of such things from an international organisation or some such source? Could he renew the request once a day? Once a week?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's practically no limit. He can make that request of the government whenever he wants to, whenever he thinks it's useful politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let's talk for a minute about the relationship between the president and the National Assembly. I think you spoke about Article 89 which, if I'm correct, deals with the president's power to decide that the National Assembly be dissolved at the proposal of the government or the cabinet. And as I understand it, the proposal has to come first from the government before the president can take any such action, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. You understood this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the government proposal you said has to be reasoned. They can't just merely request it because they don't like the National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The proposal has to be reasoned, and the reasons have to be very convincing because all this is available to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you did mention that, that the reasons had to be convincing. My question is: Convincing to whom? Convincing to the president? Convincing to the public? Both?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons had to be convincing both to the president and to the public, because this is a very strong political move for the National Assembly, which is the parliament, the expression of the national will, to be dissolved. And the citizens have to be convinced that the reasons why the president of the republic has done this at the proposal of the government are truly justified. Because it was their will that the Assembly should be of such and such a composition, that the political forces should be distributed in such and such a manner. If somebody disbands the Assembly, then the reasons have to be very strong. And so far in situations where the Assembly has been disbanded, the reasons provided were very thorough. We mentioned an instance of that sort yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say the reasons for doing it have to be strong or truly justified, do you mean that as a practical matter because of the consequences that would flow if it were perceived that the disbanding was not justified?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government decides to take such a step and to dissolve the Assembly. As a rule, the public is convinced because, of course, the term of office of the government also ceases when the Assembly is disbanded. So the public is convinced that both the government and the Assembly have lost their legitimacy, and these moves were approved by public opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the government decides to make a proposal to the president that the Assembly be dissolved, does the president have any discretion or must he pronounce the Assembly dissolved?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does have a discretionary right. He decides whether or not to dissolve the Assembly upon a reasoned proposal of the government. If he had to do it, then he would not be needed. The Assembly would be disbanded by the very fact that the government wished it to be disbanded. And in many systems, and also the system in the Federation in 1992, it was the government and not the president who dissolved the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what would happen in the situation if the president decided he wasn't satisfied with the reasons or for no reason at all he did not want to disband the Assembly. The Assembly continues and the government loses face, what happens?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly continues, that much is clear, it is not disbanded. And the government, as you put it, loses face because its public image is now sullied because the president of the republic has failed to accept its proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me turn to the constitutional provision that allows for the president to -- I think this is Article 132, the president can propose the constitution be amended. And as I understand it, he can do that on his own initiative, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, your understanding is correct, on his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the other ways of having a proposal to amend the constitution are the cabinet can do it, correct, and in your case that was a group of maybe 30 people?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the cabinet can do it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or at least 50 deputies from the National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, or at least 100.000 voters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in that relative scheme of things, the president is pretty important, because he's only one person and he can do the same thing that it takes 100.000 voters to do or 50 deputies or the entire cabinet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. As I said, the same type of solution is found in France's 1958 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Connecting this ability with his ability to request the government to state its positions on issues, those two things give him some opportunity to stir-up public opinion and perhaps bring about changes that otherwise he doesn't have the constitutional direct power to do, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand fully what changes you are talking about. Amendments to the constitution, is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I mean if the president has a position about some policy of the government cabinet or some laws issued by the National Assembly that he's not pleased with, he doesn't have any constitutional power to veto the law or remove the cabinet minister. But by mobilising popular opinion because he is the popularly elected president, by generating a lot of public debate through his ability to ask the government to state its positions and through his ability to even suggest an amendment to the constitution, that may bring pressures to bear on the cabinet and/or the National Assembly that could lead them to make certain concessions or acquiesce to a known position of the president just in order to reduce that popular outcry. Could you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is outside the constitution. This is external to the constitution. Can he mobilise the public opinion in favour of his opinion, would this public opinion be strong enough to influence the cabinet and the Assembly? All these are factual questions. There is nothing that law has to say about this. This all depends on one's personal charisma, personal magnetism, if you like. This depends on the president as a person. Is he capable of turning the public opinion around and getting it to oppose the National Assembly and the government? That is the question that we are facing here. I continue to believe that any president who is also the leader of a political party faces much better odds in communicating with the public rather than a president who does not happen to be also a party leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. President -- Professor, I think there was one typographical error in the transcript on Tuesday. At page 12977, line 14, I don't remember what the subject was but you were talking about the Federal Assembly was entrusted with electing the federal republic, and I think in that context it was the Federal Assembly was entrusted with electing the federal president. Is that correct? This would regard the 1992 Constitution for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. In the Federation, it is the Federal Assembly that elects the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, not the citizens directly and I explained why that was the case. There is a huge disproportion between the number of voters in Serbia and the number of voters in Montenegro. In the Federal Assembly, the so-called upper chamber, the federal chamber, because we are talking about the republic that is bigger than the other one, and this is used to establish an equal footing for everyone. Both members are represented by the same number of delegates, 20 each. It is impossible for a president of the republic to be elected without both republics being in agreement on the appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, that clears up a question I had. One of the other rights that the president had under the constitution was the right of suspension veto. And as I understand, if the National Assembly passes a law, the president can suspend it -- he can suspend it for seven days, is that correct? Does he have seven days after it's announced in which to say he does not want to issue it? How does that time-limit work?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, no law can be announced without the president of the republic having previously pronounced it. It is the president that promulgates a law. The seven-day deadline is taken to begin on the day a law is adopted by the National Assembly. That is when the deadline begins to run. It is within this period that the president of the republic can send the law back to the National Assembly to have another vote. This is also the mildest form of suspensive veto in comparative constitutional law. A government's legislative policy is not hereby blocked since it's the government that makes proposals for laws, on laws to the National Assembly, this simply suspends the legislative procedure for a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What vote does the National Assembly have to repass the law by, is it the same majority as normal or is there an extra requirement if the president has sent the law back?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is necessary to have the same majority, the same majority that is normally used in terms of decision-making in the Assembly. This is not a question of qualified majority. Article 80 reads: "The National Assembly decides by a majority of votes at a meeting attended by the majority of the national delegates unless the constitution stipulates a special majority to be used." Given the article that you mentioned, and I believe that was Article 84, there is no talk of a special majority there which means the normal majority is what it takes at a meeting attended by the majority of the total number of national delegates. Therefore, the same sort of majority that previously adopted the now-vetoed law in the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Professor, that in real life the suspension of a law taking effect for seven days could under certain circumstances have a significant effect or impact. For example, if, going back historically, on March the 20th, 1999, the National Assembly had passed a particular law and President Milutinovic had exercised his power here to send it back, by the 23rd of March, before seven days are up, the state of war has been declared then the National Assembly is not meeting. What happens to that law then, it's not a law because it was passed but it was then sent back by the president and the National Assembly didn't have a chance to vote on it afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We were really patient, but this is calling for speculation, Your Honour. This is the third or fourth question along these lines. What would have happened if this has happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, theories are always important when one is dealing with expert evidence, and this seems to me to be a different question from any that have been asked so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we're all agreed that the question is permissible and we shall repel the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please answer the question now, Professor, and tell us what would have happened to a law sent back on the 20th of March once the National Assembly was unable to meet.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, as far as I know, President Milutinovic - and I'm quite certain - never used suspensive veto throughout his time in office he never once used this power under Article 84. Hypothetically speaking what would have happened, well you know that in the system of your own country there is such a thing as a pocket veto, a special institute. The president of the republic puts the law in his own pocket to all practical intents and then what one has to do is wait for the next session of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you used the expression "pocket veto" there and it's been omitted from the transcript. Please continue. Is there anything else you want to say on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, if that happens there is no Assembly. One waits for the Assembly to convene, and the same type of situation is found in the law of his country where the president puts the law into his own pocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. One other presidential power that I -- I was still a bit confused about was the power to confer decorations and awards under Article 83, I think that's item number 10 in the list of 12. And we had the discussion about the Law on Ranks, I guess, and General Lukic's promotion. Under that constitution and after that constitutional decision that -- the Constitutional Court's decision, did the president of Serbia still have any power to confer decorations and awards?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, a correction. A rank is no decoration. A rank is no award. Decoration is something different altogether. For the president to be able to exercise this particular power, it is necessary for a law to provide for the types of decorations and awards that exist in the Republic of Serbia. Since this law was never passed, all that was left was the normative possibility which never materialised. Even the now-President of the republic Boris Tadic is still unable to award decorations and grant awards because this law has not been passed yet. There is the law in the Federation which was later taken over by the state union of Serbia and Montenegro, based on which the then-president and then the future president of the state union between Serbia and Crna Gora; for example, Mr. Svetozar Marovic awarded decorations but Mr. Tadic stated explicitly that he did not wish to award any medals or decorations based on a law that had been adopted for the Federation. He said he wouldn't do this before a law was passed by the Republic of Serbia to cover this matter. Likewise, Mr. Milutinovic could not have awarded any decorations or awards; only the federal president could have done something like that. For example, President Milosevic during his term in office did, indeed, award decorations and awards, but he did that in his capacity as the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In his capacity as the president of the Republic of Serbia, he never awarded a single decoration or medal simply because there was no foundation for anything like that in the law as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in Serbia between 1992 and 2000, even though there was this constitutional provision as a practical matter, there wasn't any law to implement it; so President Milutinovic, for example, couldn't decorate or issue awards to anybody, even though he had the power but there wasn't any implementing law in place. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But for purposes of trying to assess, analyse, the constitution and decide whether or not it provides for a strong president or a weak president or something in between, let me ask you this hypothetical because I think on page 12990 you were talking about the president not having any special powers over state administration. If there had been a law in place under which President Milutinovic could issue decorations and awards, isn't that something that a president could use that could have an impact on how things were done in the country. If, for example, he showered awards and decorations on a particular ministry or a particular state institution, that could engender some rivalry within those agencies in the state. Couldn't that have a real-life effect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours, the objection is the same. If a law had been in place, would have this happen or that happen, it clearly calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand the reason why you object here, but bear in mind the beginning of this question which is to put it in the context of analysing the overall effect of these provisions in relation to the status and power of the president. So taking account of that, we'll allow the question. We're perfectly capable of deciding in due course whether the answer is of value or of no value.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Rather, Professor, can you deal with that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on what I know about the law on decorations and awards, a proposal must always come from an authorised proposer, so to speak, the Serbian Academy of Sciences, one of the universities, institutions of that sort of stature. It is not for the president of his own accord to award certain decorations. There is a procedure in place and the same applies to pardons. There is a specific procedure in place for both. You talk about showering someone with decorations. In that case, the president would compromise his own reputation as well as the very institute of awarding decorations and medals, it would constitute a clear misuse. There has to be an opinion that prevails in terms of the person in question being someone generally believed to merit decoration. For example, President Svetozar Marovic decorated the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church, Pavle, the patriarch Pavle. These are public figures who certainly merit some form of recognition. It isn't as if the president were in a position to shower with favours or decorations people that he simply likes. Maybe that would constitute a violation of the constitution because the very spirit of the constitution would, in this case, be betrayed or violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I understand the sense of the notion that there should be some -- some protocol and some standards with regard to issuing awards or decorations, but at the time there wasn't any implementing law, correct? So I'm not sure what you talk about in your answer --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's move on to the power of the National Assembly and the president to ask for reports from the Ministry of Interior. Do you recall that discussion on Tuesday, I think that was at transcript page 12991? Do you recall that article I think? I don't have the tab cite for it, but I think it relates to the Law on the Interior or the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. As far as I remember, because by now the tape prevails, I think this is Article 9 on the Law on the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's tab 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I please have the exhibit number again, we do not have tabs so the tab numbers do us no good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Did -- do you read that to mean that both the president and the National Assembly have to request the report? It has to be a joint request. I think that was what you testified to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be the conclusion suggested by a linguistic interpretation. Otherwise, it would have been an alternative to the request made by the National Assembly or the president of the republic, and then it is the minister's responsibility and so on and so forth. But here it says: "At the request of the National Assembly and the president of the republic," so this is cumulative, it's a joint request by both the National Assembly and the president of the republic. The particle "and" suggests that there have to be requests by both parties. Were it just one of the parties making the request, it would be worded in the following way: "The National Assembly or the president of the republic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So the Ministry of Interior under that reading would be justified in refusing a request from just the president alone, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want my personal view, I think this article is unconstitutional, but this wasn't confirmed by the Constitutional Court. I don't think it should be part of this law. However, it found its way into the law and no one ever brought up the issue of its constitutionality. Excuse me, I am getting increasingly tired, so I forget what exactly your question was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. My question was: Could the ministry refuse to provide a report if it was only the president asking for it and the National Assembly didn't join in the request?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is no request then, is there? At least that's what the particular wording seems to suggest. A request can only come about if made by both of these players: The National Assembly and the president of the republic, jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your earlier answer you said that in your personal view you think this law is unconstitutional. What about it do you find to be unconstitutional?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean the law in its entirety. I meant this article. The unconstitutional element is precisely what we addressed when you asked me at the very outset about the nature of the powers of the president of the republic, the powers of the president of the republic are a constitutional category. It is not possible to amplify these by law. What we see here is that the president of the republic is granted by law a power not granted to him by the constitution. More importantly, the National Assembly is granted a power not granted by the constitution. By this token, the constitutional provision is violated which specifies that the president covers other areas, too, but only those provided for in the constitution and nothing beyond that. You see, turning to the National Assembly, Article 73. Article 73, the last item, item 13, the same sort of wording as we find in the portion related to the president of the republic carries out other tasks in keeping with the constitution, which means that even the Assembly must not be granted powers by law alone. This is a law granting a certain power to the Assembly, but it is the Assembly that creates the law, that produces the law, and that is the reason this law no longer applies. No need to point that out, I suppose, but it's unconstitutional because it's not in keeping with Article 73 or 83. It grants both the Assembly and the president of the republic powers not granted them by the constitution. The constitution is clear. Both the Assembly and the president of the republic have only those powers granted them by the constitution. I'm not sure if this article can actually be applied in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just the transcript, Your Honour. Page 68, line 3 or 4, it says with Article 73 or 83. The Professor said 73, 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 73, 13, thank you. Professor, in relation to the second part of that answer that the article would be unconstitutional in relation to giving power to the National Assembly to seek a report from the minister, is it not their right as the body responsible for the appointment of the minister in the first place to call for reports? Is that not what parliamentary democracy is all about? And I'm separating that from your point in relation to the president.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the very essence of parliamentary democracy, and it also follows from the constitution. However, any type of control power in relation to the ministries is something that the cabinet enjoys. They can't request reports from the ministries. They can validate or annul certain documents produced by the ministries. The National Assembly can institute a vote of confidence on a specific minister or the cabinet as a whole. The minister can be recalled, or rather, the revocation of a certain minister can be proposed to the Assembly by the cabinet itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The Law on Internal Affairs must have been proposed by the cabinet to the National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And surely, therefore, that is the cabinet ceding to the National Assembly authority to go directly to that ministry? I find it difficult to see what's unconstitutional about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The unconstitutional thing is the National Assembly as a constitutional category. No law should deal with the National Assembly or grant it powers for that matter. This power of the National Assembly is embodied in Article 73 of the constitution, paragraph 11. It talks about the control that the Assembly exercises over the work of the government and other officials responsible for their work to the National Assembly in keeping with the law and the constitution. It is not fair, if I may put it that way in purely legal terms for the law to repeat something that is already stated in the constitution, because the dignity of the norm itself is violated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But surely Article 73, 11 would give the National Assembly power to seek a report from the government about the work of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, but this is not what it says in terms of language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just bear with me. If that's the case, if the National Assembly are entitled to ask the government to report and all these laws are made at the suggestion of the government, is it not perfectly within their power to say, Well, when you do that in relation to the Ministry of the Interior, you can do it directly? And if I could just take it a little further, if that's right then to add the president to that situation would be in a sense restricting the National Assembly's freedom to seek such a report, and therefore might be seen as a way in general of the government saying in relation to Ministry of Interior, this is how you can go about it seeking information from us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree with you, but all of that means that the constitution should be there. And it's not right from a legal standpoint that what the constitution says is repeated in the law, especially in such a modified manner. All of that is stated in the constitution in Article 73, item 11, and now it was modified by the law asking that there be a simultaneous request and a mutual request by the National Assembly and the president of the republic. From that point of view, the constitution was modified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I want to follow on the other side of that. Judge Bonomy was asking you about the National Assembly's right to request that information under that provision of the Law on the Interior. Professor, if you as a constitutional lawyer and a good lawyer were trained to try to argue both sides of a point, if you were representing President Milutinovic, if you were representing President Milutinovic in a situation like this where you were trying to argue that, yes, as president I am entitled under the constitution to request these reports from the Ministry of Interior, as set out in this provision of the law, and it's not an unconstitutional extension of my powers, couldn't you argue: Rather, it is part of my powers under the constitutional provision that allow me to request the government to express its opinions and as part of the catch-all provision under Article 83, 12, to conduct other affairs in accordance with the constitution? Because if I can ask the entire government for its position, then this is merely one ministry within the government. Could you make that argument with a straight face, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely that is the meaning of my point, that all of this is embodied in the constitution in Article 85, when the government is requested to take a position, the Ministry of Internal Affairs is under the government; then -- well, the Ministry of the Interior is one of the ministries in the government. And yet again, as I've already said, the National Assembly has authority to exercise control over the work of the entire government, therefore, one of its ministries as well. Singling out only the Ministry of the Interior in this way and not any other ministry is not right from the point of view of the constitution. That is my point. Why say that when all of that is already incorporated in Article 85 and Article 73, respectively? And all of it is put in language that is not identical to that put in the constitution; namely, in terms of the president of the republic and the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move on to the SDC and some new topics and I think we went a couple minutes long this morning and the Professor and I are growing increasingly tired, I wonder if we could take a recess a couple minutes early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Hannis. We will adjourn now, Professor, for lunch and see you again at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.43 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I know it's been a long week and we're in the last session for this week. If at any time you want to take a break, please let us know. I want to move now to the president of the republic's role in connection with the supreme -- or with the Supreme Defence Council. You mentioned in your testimony on Tuesday that that was a position he held ex officio, Mr. Milutinovic, that is. Can you tell us regarding your knowledge, who were the members of the Supreme Defence Council in 1998 and 1999 -- well, I guess I should say 1988 [sic] and 1999 up until the 23rd of March, because I understand the rules of procedure were changed on the 23rd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, the members of the Supreme Defence Council were the following: The president of the Federal Republic, Slobodan Milosevic; the president of the Republic of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic; and the president of the Republic of Montenegro, I have forgotten his name, Mile Djukanovic, yes. I didn't make that big a mistake, did I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1999, March 23rd, when there were introduced a change to the rules of procedure for the SDC, did that rule change or those rules changes provide for additional persons to attend SDC meetings? Whether they were members or not we'll talk about in a minute.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. New persons were added precisely again ex officio. However, their status was interesting. They could not have the status of a member. Members of the Supreme Defence Council were spelled out in the constitution. These people had to attend sessions ex officio. It was the federal minister of defence, the Chief of General Staff, and if I'm not mistaken, the federal prime minister, but I'm not sure. They had to attend sessions according to the provisions of the rules of procedure from the 23rd of March, 1999. This is an interesting provision. In a way it corrects Article 135 of the constitution, because Article 135 of the constitution says in paragraph 2 only on the members of the Supreme Defence Council in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I guess considering the circumstances at the time, the 23rd of March, on the eve of war, it might make sense to expand the attendees of the Supreme Defence Council to include the minister of defence and the head of the General Staff of the army, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It would have made sense, in view of the subject matter that the Supreme Defence Council dealt with and in view of the fact that members of the SDC were there ex officio. And as for the offices they held, there were other criteria that prevailed, not military criteria. However, these people who became members certainly could not take part in decision-making because this would be in direct contravention of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, then, Professor, after the 23rd of March, even though now the minister of defence and the head of the General Staff of the army or their representatives are required to attend meetings, but in effect they're not really voting members of the SDC. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it would have been to be. On the basis of the constitution, they do not have the rights of members because the constitution does not recognise them as members of the Supreme Defence Council. They can only contribute to the quality of the discussion on certain items that were on the agenda of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, of course, Professor, you, yourself, never personally attended an SDC meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. No. I was not qualified in any way for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you never had a chance to see the full stenographic minutes of -- or the stenographic notes of any of those meetings, have you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I did have occasion to do that. As for all the stenographic notes from sessions held in 1997 and 1998, and at one session in 1999, I read them very carefully while preparing for this responsibility that I'm discharging before you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me be sure I understand. Did you see the verbatim stenographic notes of the meetings or did you see the minutes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the stenographic notes, too, and the minutes. When there were only minutes and no stenographic notes, then I saw only the minutes. But when there were stenographic notes taken, too, then I saw both the stenographic notes and the minutes. Everything I saw is contained in the documentation, I think, related to my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall for which of the meetings you actually had access to verbatim accounts in the stenographic minute -- stenographic notes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw them for the session of the 28th of October, 1997, then for all sessions during 1998 and the session held on the 23rd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one minute. Your Honour, I believe there is some confusion here. Maybe it would be easier if the documents to which the Professor is referring are shown to him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean just for the purposes of clarity, because I'm not sure that -- because Professor said that actually all the documents that he has seen are within these binders that we have provided to the parties. So therefore, I think just for the purposes of clarity it would be easier if -- I can provide the numbers as well, if my learned friend wants --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's for Mr. Hannis to decide at this stage how to conduct --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And obviously you can deal with it in whatever way you wish in re-examination. But if he wishes to do so at the moment, no doubt he'll be grateful for your assistance on references.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think at the moment, Professor, I'm going to maybe come back to that. But to your understanding, what you looked at is contained in the binders and there's nothing you looked at concerning the SDC that's not contained in the binders?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is contained in the binders, but even if it's not, while preparing for this testimony I informed myself because I read all the minutes, not only read them, I studied them, studiously, and I told you where I started from. The first one I read is from the 28th of October, 1997. I read all the minutes from the sessions held in 1998 and stenographic notes as well, and this one record, the minutes from the session held on the 23rd of March, 1999. I did not read the minutes up to 1997, Mr. Milosevic not being president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I did not read them for after 1999 because in the period from 1999 up to October 2000, there were no sessions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask a question this way regarding, for example, the documents you looked at concerning the meeting for the 23rd of March, 1999. Was -- did you just look at one document, whether it was the minutes or the stenographic notes, or did you look at two separate documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for some sessions, there were two different documents, but as far as I can remember for that session, the 23rd of March, 1999, there weren't any stenographic notes, it was only minutes. That is my recollection. After all, strain takes its toll, doesn't it, and I forget some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Professor, believe me. Who showed you those documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these documents I received from the Defence in order to prepare for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you still have the ones that were provided to you to review?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned that to the Defence because I looked through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you return them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I returned them, I think, here, in The Hague --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because it involves lots of luggage. I had a suitcase full of documentation and I don't have the physical strength to return all of that to Belgrade, so I returned it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Here, shortly before you testified at the beginning of this week?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this week, upon my arrival in The Hague, and I arrived in The Hague on the 20 -- no, sorry, 30 -- on the 30th of July this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Professor. I want to ask you a question about a comment you made on Tuesday at page 13004 of the transcript. I think Mr. Zecevic was asking you about the Article 133 of the federal constitution and the army's duty to defend the constitutional order. And he gave you a hypothetical, and you agreed that that would constitute an attack on the constitutional order. You said: "Because everything that changes or wishes to change something by extra-constitutional means, that is to say, apart from regular procedure, that's an attack on the constitutional order." Now, I want to ask you a question related to that definition and that understanding. Professor, are you familiar -- or I will tell you that there have been some evidence in this case, some allegations, that in March 1989, when the issue of amending the constitution of Serbia was being discussed by the Assembly in Kosovo, there is some evidence that suggest that during that event there were tanks stationed around the Assembly building, that inside the Assembly hall itself there were some uniformed VJ members, there was some police, there were persons in civilian clothes who were not members of the Assembly sitting in, allegations that some of those nonmembers actually raised their hands when the vote was taken, and that there was no count made on the record of the votes. If, hypothetically speaking, that evidence were all true, would you agree with me that that was an example of a change by extra-constitutional means?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could agree with you, had I not watched on television in Belgrade the testimony of Mr. Vukasin Jokanovic, who was president of the Assembly of Kosovo and Metohija at that time, and who showed through a film how the vote took place in the Assembly. And as a direct witness, as the president of the Assembly, he testified that the constitutionally prescribed majority was attained. I was not present at that Assembly, but I fully believe that when the president of the Assembly shows this, who not only saw this with his own eyes but chaired the meeting and ex officio, as president of the Assembly, he was supposed to see whether there was a quorum in the Assembly, whether there were enough MPs present to vote and to see whether everything was carried out constitutioni artis, in accordance with the constitution, as required by the constitution. Now, if this assumption of yours is taken into account, then what you say would have been the case, an extra-constitutional change of the constitutional order. However, this time according to the statement of Mr. Jokanovic and what he showed, the change was fully in keeping with the constitution. After all, he testified under oath. He showed a film showing all of this. We could all see this when he testified in the proceedings against President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: One question, I'm sorry, to ask. Did he say anything about the Assembly being encircled by tanks and troops? Did the president of the Assembly say anything on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, I just watched the TV broadcast. I could not say anything with any degree of certainty, but I know that the federal Presidency at that time, the Presidency of the SFRY, and we read the conclusions of the Assembly on this, due to the special situation applied special measures. So it was a federal authority, not an authority of the Republic of Serbia. I am not able to testify about the facts here quite simply because I was not present there at the time. All of this took place in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I live in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was about to say that to you. Virtually all of your answer has been about the facts. The question is a question related to your expertise as a witness here and you answered that right at the beginning. So let's try to concentrate on what the questions are actually about. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about the army's role and what its job was to do under Article 133. You pointed out that the army is always called upon to "defend the sovereignty, the territory, the independence, and the constitutional order of the country." And at page 13005 and 6, it appeared that you agreed with Mr. Zecevic that, in your view, there wasn't any action required by some other state organ for the army to be used in case one of those four objects was threatened. Is that -- do I have that correctly? Is that your view?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, it's not my view. It's the position in the constitution which I have simply retold. But what you're referring to happened in 1989, and we are referring to a provision from 1992. So there is a time difference here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor. I didn't mean to relate this most recent question about the army to what I had asked you about events at the Assembly in Kosovo in 1989. Just as a general proposition under 133, it is your position that the army can be engaged without, for example, without declaring a state of emergency or a state of imminent threat of war or a state of war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It follows from Article 133, paragraph 1 of the constitution. The army is duty-bound to protect the sovereignty, the territory, and so on in every situation, in any state, whether regular or irregular.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I see nothing in Article 133, and if it exists somewhere else can you point me to it, that would indicate who was supposed to decide whether that condition exist; that is, that there is a threat to the sovereignty, territory, independence, or constitutional order that requires the army to leap to its defence. Is that up to the Chief of the General Staff, a commander in the field, a politician? Who decides?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision, as we saw when such states are declared, is made by the National Assembly; and if it is unable to convene, then the federal government or cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that they are the ones who decide if such a state did exist, but I guess I was taking your prior answer to mean that: No, the army could go out in the field and take actions even without the declaration of one of those states if they thought -- I guess if the army thought that there was a threat. Am I misunderstanding your prior evidence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, you're not. That's still how I understand it. I'm simply adhering to the constitution, but that's my understanding of Article 133, paragraph 1 of the constitution. There are no limitations to that paragraph. It simply says that in any situation the army shall defend the sovereignty, territory, independence, and constitutional order of the country without any limits to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But how do we interpret that in light of the provisions that indicate that the army during both peace and wartime is commanded by the president of the republic in conjunction with or in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way it's written down here. The president of the federal republic in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. I don't see what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I understood your earlier answers to indicate that the army could go out in the field to take action in defence of a perceived threat, perceived by the army, without waiting for a word or a decision from anyone else. Am I incorrect in that understanding of your prior answers?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the army has its chain of command, you can see in Article 135. And I cannot say more than that because I'm not familiar with the chain of command in the army, I'm not a military expert. I'm just telling you how it is based on the constitution, and this is how we lawyers read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I asked these questions because I think Judge Bonomy asked or made a comment yesterday that reflected my confusion at page 13007 he said: "My understanding at the moment is that without any other organ being involved, the army can itself act to defend the constitutional order on the basis that it thinks that there is some challenge being made to it and I find that strange." And so do I and that's what I need some clarification on.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly cannot command the army nor can the cabinet. Only the organ commanding the army can decide that, and in Article 135 it says who the supreme commander is. It's not the National Assembly or the government, it's rather the president of the republic, in compliance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council and I don't see any problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then now I take it then that you're saying that the army couldn't just on its own go out, but it would take some direction from the commanding authority, that is, the president of the republic, acting in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. So I guess that would be the body or the people who would have to perceive that there was a threat that required the army to defend under Article 133 of the constitution, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what follows from the text of the constitution. That's precisely what the constitution says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to that there's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did we not have evidence from you, Professor, that the right interpretation of that provision about in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council was that the president, nevertheless, could act on what he thought appropriate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that from the stenographic record one can see that the Supreme Council issued conclusions. I never read any decision, nor did I ever see any decision of the Supreme Defence Council in any official publication. But what the precise chain of command was, I don't know. When, however, I looked at the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council, nowhere did I find that the Supreme Defence Council ever issued a decision or that such a decision was ever published anywhere or that it had a name, a title, as the decisions of the president of the federal republic and the Chief of the General Staff did. We saw that there was a whole list of terms for these various documents. Here we see just the common term, the general term,"conclusion." It doesn't say what sort of decisions they could make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the Law on Defence doesn't say that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So at the end of the day the army went to war without a decision of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the conclusion reached at a session of the Supreme Defence Council of the 4th of October, 1998, was read out and it was certainly used as a basis for the army to go to war. In those conclusions, it says that Yugoslavia is committed to peace and to the peaceful resolution of all open issues. But if the country is attacked, we shall defend ourselves using all means. I think that was the conclusion issued at the session of the Supreme Defence Council of the 4th of October, 1998. As a lawyer, I feel that this is not a way to express a legal norm; it is simply a political standpoint. On the basis of this, a decision would have to be issued couched in legal terms. What does it mean to defend by all means? What means? If we are attacked, what is implied by an attack? And then the commitment to peace, those are the things political fora say, we are committed to peace and a peaceful resolution of all open issues. That's not for the Supreme Defence Council to say. The Supreme Defence Council deals with defence, not with solving open issues by peaceful means. So these are my observations that I had reading through the stenographic records and minutes of the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope you don't mind me repeating the question, which was: "So at the end of the day the army went to war without a decision of the Supreme Defence Council?" Can you answer that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because these conclusions were used in lieu of a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Professor, yesterday you were very keen to distinguish the concept of "conclusion" from the concept of "decision." It was a very important part of your -- not just yesterday, a very important part of your evidence as I understood it. Do you want to modify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm not modifying my evidence. These conclusions are evidently not a decision, but they obviously served as a decision. As a lawyer, I feel that this is not a decision, there is no decision in there, just a political attitude. But obviously it was used -- it was relied upon as if it were a decision. I still maintain what I said before and what you said now, in my view this is not a decision. But, evidently, these conclusions were used as a decision. This is just a political standpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I next want to show you a document that I don't think you've seen before. It wasn't -- at least it wasn't on the list, and this is Exhibit P717.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a hard copy, if we could hand this to the Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, this is a document in evidence here. It's a letter from General Perisic dated the 23rd of July, 1998, to President Slobodan Milosevic. You're aware, are you not, that at that time General Perisic was the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's my understanding that at some point in time this became a matter of some public discussion. Have you ever heard about this? This is a disagreement or a complaint that General Perisic had about how the army was being used and his view that it was necessary to proclaim one of the extraordinary states if the army was going to be used in Kosovo against the civilian population outside the border area or when not protecting VJ facilities and personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's just a technical issue. Can we have it on the e-court, this particular -- no, we have the first page of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think they need page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To start with. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Professor, I think I highlighted on your copy in pink the portions I wanted to ask you about specifically, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am following to see whether Mr. Hannis will put a precise question because it says here that the army is being used against the civilian population, but I'm not sure that that's what it says in the document. That's in the document Mr. Hannis was about to show the witness. Nor that there was any public debate as to whether the army was being used against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I had asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does your question require to be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my initial question was just, first of all, had the witness heard about this letter from General Perisic to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I didn't hear about it. I was not an addressee. The addressee is the president of the FRY, Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Professor, but I had some reason to think that this eventually came to be a matter of some public debate or discussion. You're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you look first at item number 1 on the first page that I've highlighted. It's -- in English it reads: "Constant tendency to use the VJ outside the institutions of the system." Is that an accurate reading of the sense of what you get from reading the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And maybe it makes more sense if I can have you read down below specific examples of the facts, if you could read then number 1 there, then we'll hear the English translation.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the text on page 161, which you underlined in red, in a red felt-tip pen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since it was highlighted, Your Honours, I think it would be more appropriate if it's put on the ELMO so we can see what my learned friend is referring to, because it is very hard for us to really understand which parts of the document Mr. Hannis is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's have it on the ELMO then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, from the top of that page, Professor, could you read what's been highlighted -- actually, could you read the entirety of the first two paragraphs there.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm very short-sighted and it's very hard for me to see this, but I will do my very best. "The tendency to use the army outside the institutions of the system. "(A) the situation in Kosovo and Metohija could have been avoided by introducing a state of emergency promptly on the 20th of April, 1998, when I submitted to you a written proposal (attachment number 1). Since this was not accepted by you, the situation has escalated and so representatives of the MUP and you too sought the use of the VJ, some smaller units were used directly and indirectly, which is, from a legal aspect, against the law, and the consequences for the state are known. "(B) so that the relevant and professional conclusions of the session of the VSO on the 9th of June, 1998, might be implemented, we requested the FRY government to provide us with (by proclaiming one of the states: Of emergency, immediate threat of war, or war) the legitimate material and financial conditions (see attachment number 2). This has not, to date, been done, which means that any engagement of the VJ in combat operations outside the border zone and beyond is still illegal and the possible consequences are unforeseeable." Should I go on reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop there, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do want to clear up one thing, Your Honours, because I can't remember when we discussed this exhibit for the first time in the Prosecution case, but you'll see in the English version item number A the second line it says: "Introducing a state of," and there's nothing else. The Professor read it and it was translated as: "State of emergency." I see the capital letters in the B/C/S and I think it does say "state of emergency," but perhaps we could clarify that either with my learned friends or through the translator; and if so, I would like to make that correction on the record regarding the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We can certainly clarify that for our learned friend but, Your Honours, we have an objection and I think maybe it would be appropriate that we don't state it in front of the witness. I mean just for the sake of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to see at the moment what your objection might be because he hasn't been asked a question yet that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in anticipation of the question, Your Honour, because the witness says he never saw the document nor is he aware of its existence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But he's an expert on this matter, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I do agree. I do agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's not being asked about matters of fact at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you still think we should have a debate out without his presence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I just wanted to state my objection along the lines which I explained; that if he's to refer to the documents which he hasn't seen, he didn't adopt it. That's the point.
