utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no reason why an expert should not be faced with other material that he hasn't necessarily seen before. In fact, that would point to a good cross-examination. I am a bit concerned that his evidence -- this passage is being disrupted unnecessarily by interventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's difficult to follow when these occur, and it's not clear at the moment that any has really assisted the situation terribly much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So back to you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if Mr. Zecevic was going to agree with me that the English should say "state of emergency."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it matters. That's how it's been translated just now. If he wants to argue about it, he'll no doubt raise it in re-examination. Let's just keep the evidence flowing, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, in item 1(A) you just read out, you see General Perisic is expressing his concern that the way the army was being used in Kosovo and Metohija was, as he said, "from a legal aspect against the law." Now, you told us earlier today that you're not an expert on matters of internal affairs or the army. General Perisic at the time was the Chief of Staff of the VJ, that is by my understanding, the highest uniform member of the army. Would you agree that he may well understand the law vis-a-vis the army better than yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If there is -- if this is a question for the expert witness, then my objection would be misplaced, but I certainly do not think that is along the lines which Your Honour just explained. That is why I find my objection suitable in anticipation of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think on this occasion Mr. Zecevic's objection is well-stated, Mr. Hannis. The -- what you're seeking is perfectly appropriate, but I don't think the way to put it is to ask for a view on Perisic's understanding of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take your point. I think it's one way to approach it, and if you're of the view that that's not the appropriate way, I will move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think you should rephrase the question. The real question here is: Has Perisic misunderstood the law? On the other hand, if your point is ultimately going to be that you would expect him -- a man in his position to have a good understanding of the law, then that's argumentative and can be dealt with later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will move on to something else at the moment and I have something to come back to on this topic later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I want to move now, Professor, to item (B) that you read out for us before, and I'll tell you what it says in English and ask you if this is correct. It says: "So that the relevant and professional conclusions of the session and the VSO," or Supreme Defence Council, "on 9 June 1998 might be implemented ..." In the English, I note that the word "conclusions" has a capital "C", which for me would suggest that "conclusions" here is being used with some sort of specificity and not in the generic sense of a conclusion and it relates specifically to 9 June 1998 meeting of the SDC. Now, you read the minutes for the 9 June 1998 meeting of the SDC, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it. There were three conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think you testified that these weren't decisions and these were only conclusions or statements of final positions, but here General Perisic is talking about implementing conclusions. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do I think is the key word here is the verb. "We requested," it's in the past tense. One thing I can tell you is that the original wording in Serbian is quite illiterate. It should read: "In order to be able to carry out or put into practice the conclusions in a responsible and professional manner from the session of the Supreme Defence Council on the 9th of June, 1998, we requested ..." How did they make these requests? It is necessary, after all, to take this conclusion and base some sort of a decision on it. Who was it that required the Serbian government to secure not legal but constitutional -- and this is the mistake. You can tell that General Perisic is no lawyer, to secure a constitutional basis, not a legal basis, to pronounce or declare special conditions as well as create the material and constitutional conditions for it. So there had to be some sort of a decision. The conclusions in purely linguistic terms are so scarce, so inadequately phrased that it was eventually necessary to operationalise the whole thing by introducing some sort of decision, which is exactly what follows from item (b). You can see that based on these conclusions the government was required or requests were made to the government to provide a legal and constitutional basis to declare one of the special states, as well as to secure material and financial conditions. We don't know what these conditions are or prerequisites because none of them are explicitly stated and in the wording is it has so far failed to do this or this has not to date been done, which means that any involvement of the JNA in combat outside the borders continues to be illegal and the consequences are unforeseeable. These are comments that I in my professional capacity as a lawyer might make facing a text like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you regarding the declaration of one of the states -- one of the extraordinary states, such as state of emergency, imminent threat of war, or state of war, I think we looked the other day with Mr. Zecevic, you were looking at the Law on Defence. I believe that's Exhibit P985, and looked at Article 4. I'm not sure what tab it is, Professor. It's tab 62 of the grey binder. Okay. Do you have that before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Do you mean me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Professor, thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Well, 62 happens to be in the other binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the usher please help Professor with the binders, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to Article 4, doesn't that call upon the -- doesn't that indicate that the declaration of one of those states of emergency shall be proclaimed. The Assembly is required to proclaim it if it determines that the sovereignty, territory, independence, or constitution are under threat. It's not a matter of discretion but it says: "The Federal Assembly shall proclaim ..."

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but an article in the constitution, and the constitution is the supreme legal act, the article in the constitution does not say that the Army of Yugoslavia shall protect the country's system in any regular state, in a state of war, or during the an imminent threat of war, but rather that the army should defend Yugoslavia regardless of the prevailing conditions. Therefore, we cannot interpret Article 133 in that way because that is not explicitly stated anywhere in the article. The army as such as an institution is called upon to defend these four values, regardless of the prevailing circumstances, regardless of whether the circumstances are normal or irregular. That is what I'm saying. And we can't imagine something as being in the constitution that is not actually there, and this simply happens to be one of those things that aren't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I'm not sure I follow that reasoning. If -- what I understood you to be saying about Article 133 was that if the army determined that there was a threat to the constitutional order, then it was required, constitutionally required, to defend the country and engage, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is my position, and any lawyer would confirm that for you having read Article 133 of the constitution. Even General Perisic does not speak about any violations of the constitution. He's using a lay term. He's here saying that the Yugoslav Army is acting outside the institutions of the system, the institutions of the system, what does that mean? What's that supposed to mean? I'm at a loss here. He's not saying that they're acting against the constitution. You see, item 1 says: "A tendency to use the army outside the institutions of the system." This phrase "the institutions of the system," well, to a lawyer that means nothing at all. What would be meaningful to a lawyer would be such phrases as "outside the constitution" or "outside the law."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, would you agree with me that if, objectively speaking, there was such a threat to the constitutional order of the country as to require the army under the constitution to engage and defend, isn't that the equivalent to what's under Article 4, that the constitution or the security of the country are under threat? And if that's the case the Federal Assembly shall proclaim one of those three extraordinary states?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the impression that I'm getting is that you relate the use of the army solely to one of these three degrees or possible irregular circumstances. If that is what you are doing, I believe you are not interpreting Article 133 of the constitution in a correct manner. My position is this: The Army of Yugoslavia can be used to defend the four objects, regardless of the fact whether the Assembly had actually proclaimed an imminent threat of war, a state of war, or a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think my difficulty lies in my understanding of what the nature of the disagreement or apparent disagreement between General Perisic and Mr. Milosevic was. Based on what he says in his letter in P717 and other evidence we've heard in this case, it appears that General Perisic, and perhaps some other individuals, took the view that absent one of those emergency states, one of those extraordinary states, that the army was to be used in the border area, the army could also be used to defend its own personnel and facilities. But General Perisic's concern was that to engage the army in combat operations against civilians and terrorists, the KLA, at least at that point in time was being referred to as the "so-called KLA," not recognised as an army but as insurgents or rebels or terrorists, General Perisic's view was that was a job for the police. If it was being done internally against the so-called KLA, it was a job for the police. And if the army was to be engaged, it was his view that a state of emergency at a minimum needed to be declared. On the other hand, it seems that Mr. Milosevic didn't want to declare a state of emergency. And you're aware, Professor, that in July of 1998, there had been some international concerns about what was happening in Kosovo. You're aware of the Security Council resolution that was passed in March. So I suggest to you, sir, that part of the problem here was that General Perisic thought that this was a political decision. He did not want the army to be engaged in this activity without a declaration of one of those states, because then he, the general, was going to be called to task. Mr. Milosevic, I suggest to you, did not want to declare one of those states because that would give the international community, perhaps, a basis for arguing that we need to come in, we need to bring foreign troops in, and help resolve this situation because Serbia can't do it on its own. Would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't, as a rule, oppose questions as long as this one, but where did my learned friend come across this, this fact that Milosevic was declaring a state of emergency? Why is he asking this question? I would be very happy if he could help me track down this particular reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question is very clear. It's based on there being no declaration of a state of emergency, so your objection is repelled. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the name is there Slobodan Milosevic refused to declare a state of emergency. That is what the whole story is about, but he cannot declare a state of emergency on top of everything else -- or at least not based on the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the Professor's view so far is that the army can act on its conclusion that there is a threat to the constitutional order. The president was the commander of the army, and therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is true, but both under regular and irregular circumstances. He's always the commander of the army, in both sets of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it is very difficult to take the line you're taking when faced with an article in the Law on Defence, which seems to provide how a state of emergency is to be declared and the view of the Professor that the constitution in Article 133 somehow or other gives a power to act as if there were a state of emergency, the equivalent of a state of emergency, without that having been declared. So in that situation, the fact that the question might not truly reflect what in the end of the day will be your position does not make it inadmissible, Mr. Fila. So this question may be answered. Mr. Hannis, I think you may have to repeat part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, do you need me to repeat my question or do you understand the essence of what I was asking you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please ask you repeat the question. I think you're overestimating me if you think I can possible memorise a question as long as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor, I know it was long-winded and let me try again. It was my understanding from this document and other evidence in the case that the dispute between -- or the disagreement between General Perisic and Mr. Milosevic boiled down roughly to this: General Perisic's view was that the army couldn't be used outside the border belt area or to defend its own personnel and facilities, could not be used against civilians within Serbia absent the declaration of a state of emergency or a state of an imminent threat of war or a state of war. And he felt that if there was a problem with the terrorists or the so-called KLA, that that was a matter to be dealt with by the MUP, by the police, because it was a matter of internal security, which was their job. And I think it's fair to suggest that he did not want the army to be doing what he saw as the police job, absent a declaration of one of those states. I suggest to you that there's evidence to support the theory that Mr. Milosevic, on the other hand, was opposed to a state of emergency being declared because Serbia was already under the watchful eyes of international observers and had already been criticised because of the perception that there was disproportionate and indiscriminate force being used against civilians in Kosovo. You had the UN resolution in March of 1998, and so this is part of the genesis of this letter from General Perisic. Would you agree with me that that's a reasonable explanation for why there is this disagreement between the two of them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know about this disagreement. My information is not first-hand, it's not even hearsay. I'm not close in any way to military matters or the army itself. However, I would understand General Perisic's position if only he could name the regulation that he's invoking. He appears to have arrived at the conclusion that this is in the very nature of things. He must invoke something specific. I don't see a specific regulation being mentioned there or invoked by General Perisic. The way I read this, this appears to be his understanding of things, based on which he then goes on to make certain proposals. Other than that, speaking of Article 4, I don't see any mention being made there of the use of Yugoslavia's army, unlike Article 133, Article 4 of the Law on Defence. Therefore, the disagreement did, in fact, exist if this was General Perisic's understanding but I don't see him invoking any specific regulations to support his theory. If President Milosevic believed what you claim he believed, then these would be two contrasting viewpoints on one and the same matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, I need to catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remind me, Professor, if in the FRY constitution there is a provision about declaring a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there is, both in the federal constitution, the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the 1992 constitution, and in the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, the 1990 Constitution--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's the 1992 constitution I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remind me of which article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's Article 78. 78, paragraph 3, and Article 99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's -- Article 99, 10. Hold on until I have a look at that. Yes. Now, that -- these two provisions are surely consistent with Article 4 of the Law on Defence, which is the law as made by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The provision is consistent with Article 78.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you say that in spite of all of that, that Article 133 gives power to the president as the supreme commander to use the army whichever way he wishes if he deems there to be some threat to the constitutional order, even though the Federal Assembly has not declared a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what I'm saying. The Army of Yugoslavia is there to defend the four values, including the constitutional order, regardless of any decisions by the Assembly. At any rate, there is no mention of any use being made of the Army of Yugoslavia in these special states. In Article 4 of the Law on Defence, these are just the criteria for the declaration of the three degrees or sets of irregular circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that suggest that ultimately Yugoslavia was a military dictatorship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't draw that conclusion myself. I'm not sure what such a conclusion could possibly be based on. There is not a single country in the world that does not defend its constitutional order or any attempts at violent, at disruption against this constitutional order. I would call such a country a country in disarray, a country which would choose not to defend its constitutional order. This would amount to anarchy. The constitution must be complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, if I understand correctly then, you seem to be saying that the army, if it perceives that there is a threat to the constitutional order, it can engage to defend, absent any declaration of one of the three extraordinary states, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because the army is commanded by the president of the republic, Mr. Milosevic, as -- and he commands in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what Article 135 of the constitution says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if you could go back to Exhibit 717 for a minute, that was the one I had given you a hard copy and marked in pink. I don't know if you still have it, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it was on the second page you had. And it was the last portion in pink that you had not read yet, and I don't know if we need to put that on the ELMO, but it's, in English: "Proposed resolution." Could you read those two paragraphs for us.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Paragraph 1 says: "The Army of Yugoslavia shall be used in a legal way to defend the border belt, military facilities, and units. The army shall not be used for any other tasks or one of the states envisaged by the constitution shall be declared and then the army shall be used to its full capacity. We understand the position, but we must have a legitimate political decision because if the Federal Assembly or the FRY government will not or is not in a position to issue it, how will anyone acquire the right to undertake this responsibility?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, is it fair to say from reading that that General Perisic seems to be taking the position that he's willing to use the army in light of what may be a perceived threat against the constitutional order, but his view is that's a political decision and it's either going to come from the Federal Assembly by declaring one of the extraordinary states or he needs it to come from the government?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand General Perisic. He sat on the Supreme Defence Council. He is a homo-duplex. This session took place on the 9th of June, 1998. He took a vote on two decisions - can we look at those decisions, please - conclusions, and he voted on the conclusion that the Army of Yugoslavia would react and intervene in an inadequate manner, as it reads, should terrorist activities by the Albanian separatist movement escalate. I am -- can only claim that this is a verbatim quote from the session and he was there. The third conclusion. It also says: "The Army of Yugoslavia shall be prepared in the case of an intervention by foreign troops, regardless of the reasons for such intervention." I would really like us to go through these conclusions, to read them out, so that I don't have to tell you about them. At the meeting, and that's what the minutes reflect, General Perisic was there. And in this letter, he claims something completely different. He was one man at the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council, and we see him wearing an entirely different hat in his letter to the president. The least I can say of him is that he is a dual personality or a homo-duplex. If you have the conclusions handy, I think that would be very helpful. He was there. Not only that, he opened the meeting, he introduced the meeting. The first conclusion of the president of the Supreme Defence Council, Mr. Milosevic, adopts the contribution of General Perisic, Chief of the General Staff. That is the very first conclusion, and this one is followed by the other two that I mentioned on the use of the Army of Yugoslavia, as it reads: "Should the terrorist activities by the Albanian separatist movement escalate," and then secondly: "On the use of the Army of Yugoslavia in the eventuality of an attack by foreign troops".

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I think that's tab 54..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the Tab 54 is the relevant document which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There. I can read it for you. This is the session held on the 9th of June, 1998. Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic was there in his capacity as Chief of the General Staff. He opened the meeting. He gave introduction. It was in his presence and with his approval that the following was said: "In relation to this item on the agenda, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic, proposed and the council unanimously adopted," unanimously, which means there was no position by General Perisic, "the following conclusions: First, we accept the introduction made by the Chief of the General Staff, this same General Perisic; secondly, should the terrorist activities by the Albanian separatist movement escalate, the Army of Yugoslavia," you see, mind the wording, "the Army of Yugoslavia will react in an adequate matter. "Thirdly, the Army of Yugoslavia shall be prepared to counter any form of foreign intervention, potentially jeopardising the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." It is quite obvious that within a month's time General Perisic seems to have entertained two entirely different position on one and the same issue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to know that we did not have the original text read out by the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I in that regard ask you two things. I understood that General Perisic would not have a vote on the Supreme Defence Council. Am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are not wrong. He could not vote, but he did not state his opposition either. Look at his introductory remarks, just look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a second then. In the conclusion of his interpretation, General Perisic underlined - and you'll see the very end of that is: "In case of an external danger, we have to mobilise the military forces," whereas the Supreme Council of Defence and other federal organs have to bring that decision." What do you think he meant by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what he meant was probably the mechanism of decision-making, commanding the army, as established in Article 135, where it says that the Army of Yugoslavia is commanded by the president of the Supreme Defence Council, or rather, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in accordance with decisions made by the Supreme Defence Council. I think that is what he meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And don't you read his letter in July as complaining that no decisions have actually been made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His letter looks like a complaint to me against the Federal Assembly and the federal government, especially the federal government. Why it did not introduce one of those states of an irregular situation and why it did not provide proper material and financial conditions. So on this particular page that I'm looking at, which is page number 2, he complains about the federal government. He says here: "In order to carry out responsibly and professionally conclusions from the Supreme Defence Council, we called upon the government to ensure for us legal and material financial conditions." Well, it's not really legal conditions, it's the constitution as I already said, material and financial. Even until now, it has not done this which means that any engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia in combat operations outside the border belt is still illegal." That is to say, that as for the legality of the engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia he sees that in previous decisions of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm trying to say is that the main objection it seems, on the basis of this letter sent by General Perisic, is that the federal government did not do two things. Firstly, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That I understand, but at the very end you've said -- perhaps it's translation: "That is to say, that as for the legality of the engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia, he sees that in previous decisions of the federal government." Is that an accurate translation of what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He has no objections as for the Supreme Defence Council. That is what it seems like on the basis of this. His objections are addressed to the federal government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, you've already made the very clear point that these three conclusions are too vague to amount to decisions. Now, what's wrong in that context with General Perisic wanting decisions made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I just stated that in the conclusions it was stated that irrespective of the situation, the Army of Yugoslavia would intervene appropriately, as it says here, "in case terrorist activities of the Albanian separatist movement escalate." In this letter, General Perisic says that the Army of Yugoslavia can be used legally only for "defending the border belt, military facilities, and units." As for other tasks, that is to say interventions against terrorist activities of the Albanian separatist movement, in his opinion, the army cannot be used for that because before that one of the three situations or states envisaged in the constitution has to be declared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, whether he's right or wrong about that is not the issue at the moment. The issue that you're highlighting -- well, your opinion you're highlighting is that there's an inconsistency in his position within a month. Now, is it not possible that he viewed the three conclusions as statements of policy, for the implementation of which it would be necessary to have executive decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the way I understand this. What I see here is that General Perisic within a month's time had different views on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can start on this next document, which relates to what we've just been talking about in 1574, but I don't know if we'll get very far. Would you like me to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we bring up Exhibit P1000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Chowhan, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I apologize. I'm sorry. This is something which is in line with what Judge Bonomy had said. May I request you -- I'm sorry, learned Professor. May I request you to kindly advert to the minutes of the 6th Session of the SDC of 4th October 1998. May I further request you to kindly go to page 6, and the last paragraph. This is tab 55, please. Yes, did you get it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: The last paragraph. Just read this and could you further enlighten us on the position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If page 6 in the English version and page 6 in the Serbian version are the same, I'm going to read this out to you, and you are going to tell me if I'm reading it out wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find the document, could it please be placed on e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please, until we get it on e-court. For the interpreters, apparently it's on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: "The Chief of General Staff by a" -- it begins from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you read that now, please, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, I can see that. "Again the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, General Perisic, took the floor by saying that he accepts the opinion that the resolution of the present situation has to be found in a political approach lest there be air-strikes. But as a soldier who is responsible according to the constitution and his own conviction to protect his country, he suggests that the Federal Assembly bring a clear decision on whether the country should enter war or not in case we are attacked."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what he said on the 4th of October. The 4th of October. That's when he said that, after the letter, after the letter that he sent, that he sent on the 23rd of July, the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, the minutes of the SDC for June the 9th that you looked at, those were minutes, correct, those are not stenographic verbatim transcripts of every word that was said by those attending the meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd really have to have a look, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's tab 54.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct, you're right. But it says at the end, stenographic notes are an integral part of these minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So does it follow from that, Professor, that we have here in tab 54 the whole of what you have read in relation to the meeting of the 5th Session on the 9th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that's not what it means. That means that we have minutes. The minutes are the essence of what was going on and how this went on word for word, verbatim, that is in the stenographic notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These then are not before us, in that case. So where are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, did -- were they among the documents you returned to the Defence at the beginning of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could not state that with any degree of certainty because there were a lot of sessions involved. It was an entire book, so to speak. Some, indeed, contained the stenographic notes and conclusions and some had only the conclusions. I cannot say just off the cuff what the situation was for this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can confirm that we don't have anything else except what we have put in here, which are the minutes. I don't -- I'm not sure to what Professor is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Professor, have you studied other material, apart from what was given to you by Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just looked at what Mr. Zecevic had given me, but in this material there are stenographic notes, too, not only conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean not only minutes, or rather -- well, yes, yes. I think that the session from the 28th of September -- no, sorry, October, the session of the 28th of October, 1997, was in the form -- I think I'm actually sure of this, in the form of stenographic notes when elements of the military budget were referred to, a very lengthy text otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have all the binders at my place, so -- I mean if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you were wondering what you would do at the weekend, Mr. Zecevic, so now you know. Well, we've reached the end of today's hearing. You may have found it a long week, Professor, however you now have a break until Monday, when we shall see you again to recommence at 9.00 on Monday morning. Please bear in mind particularly at the weekend to avoid discussing the evidence in this case with anyone. Enjoy it thinking of other matters and come back refreshed on Monday, ready to start at 9.00. Now you can please leave with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you asked me about the Sainovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- motion seeking leave to amend Rule 65 ter submission. We had filed an objection concerning the written statement of Mr. -- General Vasiljevic yesterday, but otherwise we don't have any objections to these proposed changes and terms of order of witnesses and length of time, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of the position in relation to Vasiljevic, which we will have to think about before dealing with it. But I don't think the application by Mr. Fila requires much thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, we will allow you to amend the 65 ter list, as requested. We shall now adjourn until 9.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.32 p.m.,
